pf2e.mechanics: Holds eight light items. Retrieving one is a single Interact action, and stowed vials and flasks don't break from falls or from being knocked prone.

at_the_table: On a night of rain, altitude, or frost, this is the difference between a real long rest and a miserable one.
A character who lends theirs to a sick companion is making a visible, costly kindness.
items.description: Dense-woven wool over an oiled canvas shell, with a lanolin smell that never quite washes out. The stitching is double-run and the ties are leather rather than cord — the mark of an outfitter who expects the buyer to actually sleep outdoors, not just own the option.
items.hooks: The best fine bedrolls in the region carry the burned brand of a single workshop — and its owner recently stopped filling orders. Anyone selling a "new" one now is selling stolen stock.
items.name: Fine Bedroll

dnd5e.mechanics: Advantage on saving throws against exhaustion caused by sleeping in rough conditions.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 circumstance bonus to Fortitude saves against environmental cold while resting.

at_the_table: The party stops being tourists and starts being an expedition: every hex they cross is now worth coin to somebody.
A finished map is a negotiable document. Who gets to buy it — the duchy, the mining consortium, the people who live there — is a session.
items.description: Ivory-nibbed pens, a brass sighting compass that swings true and stops dead, and inks that smell faintly of walnut and iron — including one that shifts from blue to black as it dries, so you can see at a glance what was drawn today. The vellum sheets are pre-ruled with hairline graticules by a hand steadier than most. Tucked in the lid is a printed table of chart-house rates, folded and refolded to softness.
items.hooks: A chart-house pays standing rates for surveys of a particular stretch of coast, and has for eleven years. It has bought the same coastline more than thirty times, from thirty different hands, and files every copy without comparing them. The clerk who accepts submissions is not curious, and is paid well not to be.
items.name: Fine Cartographer's Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as cartographer's tools. You have advantage on checks to produce an accurate map and on Wisdom (Survival) checks to avoid becoming lost in terrain you have mapped with this kit. A finished map meets chart-house standards and sells as a trade good (typically 5–25 gp, more for unmapped territory).

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as artisan's tools (cartography). You gain a +1 item bonus to Survival checks to Sense Direction in terrain you have mapped with this kit, and maps you Craft with it are salable goods (typically 5–25 gp, more for uncharted regions).

at_the_table: The cliff nobody sane attempts becomes the entrance nobody guards.
Rigging a line so the whole party — and the injured hostage — can descend is competence made visible. Let the climber narrate it.
items.description: A waxed-leather harness that creaks like a good saddle, forged ascender cams that bite rope with a clean ratcheting snick, and pitons blued so they don't wink sunlight off a cliff face. The rope runs through your hands without a single splinter of stray fiber. Every strap end is whip-stitched in red thread — an outfitter's habit borrowed from the practice of marking gear that has already held a falling body once.
items.hooks: You can buy the kit off the shelf, but the red-thread stitching is added afterward, one strap at a time, by an old rigger the outfitter keeps on for exactly this. He stitches white thread on gear he expects to come back. He used red on yours without measuring, weighing, or asking where you were headed.
items.name: Fine Climbing Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as a climber's kit (while anchored, you can't fall more than 25 feet from the anchor point). Anchoring or unanchoring yourself is a bonus action rather than an action, and a set anchor doesn't pull free on a failed Strength (Athletics) check to climb.

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as a climbing kit (+1 item bonus to Athletics checks to Climb while one hand is free to work the gear). Setting or releasing an anchor is a single Interact action, and on a critically failed check to Climb while anchored, the anchor holds — you fall no farther than the anchor allows.

at_the_table: Wherever there's water, the ration count stops mattering — which changes every wilderness route the party is willing to consider.
An hour of fishing is the genre's confession booth. Put two characters on the bank with one kit and the backstory arrives on its own.
items.description: The wallet unrolls with a smell of oiled leather and dried waterweed, each lure pinned in its own loop: bright feather for fast water, dull horsehair for still, a silver-wired minnow for the deep cold. The lines are silk-cored and knotless where cheaper kits are all splices. Inside the flap, a previous owner has inked a map of one river's pools — and crossed out the last one.
items.hooks: Whoever ties these lures uses feathers from a marsh bird the riverfolk swear went silent a generation ago. The new lures keep coming, a fresh dozen every season, and the feathers are always this year's molt.
items.name: Fine Fishing Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: A rolled leather wallet of lines, hooks, weights, hand net, and two dozen tied lures sorted by water and season. With 1 hour at any waterway, a DC 10 Wisdom (Survival) check yields a day's food for one creature, plus one additional creature for every 2 points by which the check exceeds the DC.

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as fishing tackle. Its sorted, hand-tied lures grant a +1 item bonus to Survival checks to Subsist at any waterway, and a success while using the kit feeds one additional creature.

at_the_table: The stealth climb is the whole point: no clang off the parapet, no second throw waking the garrison.
Sentries know the sound of a normal hook. The absence of that sound is worth ten gold to anyone who works at night.
items.description: Three forged tines fold flat against the shaft like a sleeping bird, and each one is wrapped in boiled felt where it will kiss stone. Flicked open, they lock with a click you feel rather than hear. The eye is welded, not bent — this hook has never let go of anything it caught.
items.hooks: A second-story crew has hit four counting-houses this season, and the only evidence left behind is a row of neat felt fibers on each windowsill. The fence who sells these hooks keeps a ledger of buyers — and has started charging for silence, too.
items.name: Fine Grappling Hook

dnd5e.mechanics: Folding tines lock open silently. When thrown to catch a ledge, a miss makes no more noise than a dropped coin, and once set, the hook doesn't slip on a climbing check that fails by 4 or less.

pf2e.mechanics: As a grappling hook; its felt-wrapped, locking tines make no noise on a missed throw, and it doesn't come loose on a failed (but not critically failed) Athletics check to Climb.

at_the_table: The fighter goes down in the mud, and this kit is the difference between "you'll live" and "you'll live, and you'll dance at your sister's wedding."
Opening it in a plague-struck village makes the party the most important people in town before anyone rolls anything.
items.description: The case opens flat and smells of clean linen, spirits, and dried yarrow. Curved needles ride in waxed paper, the silk thread is sorted by gauge, and every dressing is rolled tight enough to drum a finger on. One interior pocket holds a small mirror and a comb — because a surgeon who sends a patient back to their family presentable has clearly lost patients before.
items.hooks: Every kit from this assembler includes one vial the label calls "last resort," stoppered in black wax. The apothecaries who stock the kits can price every other item in the case. None of them will say what the vial costs, or what it does, and none of the used kits that come back for refilling still have it.
items.name: Fine Healer's Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as a healer's kit with 10 uses. You have advantage on Wisdom (Medicine) checks to diagnose an ailment, treat a wound, or perform field surgery while the kit is in hand, and a creature you stabilize with it wakes without infection or scarring from that wound.

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as healer's tools of expanded quality: +1 item bonus to Medicine checks to Administer First Aid, Treat Disease, Treat Poison, and Treat Wounds.

at_the_table: The mechanical benefit is small; the *forensic* one is the real product. "No tool marks" means the theft isn't discovered until inventory day — and the party's timeline for being elsewhere just grew by a week.
Sixty gold for picks is also a character statement: this isn't a hobby anymore.
items.description: A doeskin roll of tempered steel picks, tension bars, and a folding mirror-probe, each tool blued dark so nothing glints at a keyhole. The tips are polished to a jeweler's finish — steel this smooth leaves a lock's pins exactly as it found them. The roll ties with a bootlace, because a silk ribbon would say too much.
items.hooks: Only two locksmiths in the region can temper picks to this finish, and both file a burr signature into the tension bar — insurance, they call it. When jobs go wrong, the signatures tell investigators which smith to lean on. Neither smith mentions this at sale.
items.name: Fine Lockpicks

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as thieves' tools. The tempered picks don't snap or jam on a failed check, and a lock opened with them shows no scratches or tool marks on later inspection.

pf2e.mechanics: As infiltrator thieves' toolkit-adjacent quality: replacement picks never break on a critically failed Pick a Lock attempt, and a lock you open bears no visible tool marks.

at_the_table: Rain starts mid-scene, and the tent is up before the argument about whether to make camp is finished.
In hostile country, an ordinary tent cracks and booms all night like a slow drum. This one lets the party sleep dark, quiet, and close to the thing they're stalking.
items.description: Tight-woven sailcloth that goes drum-taut on its poles and stays that way — you can lay a palm against the wall in a gale and feel the wind pass over without a single snap of canvas. The seams are lapped and waxed the way shipwrights waterproof a hull, and one corner grommet has been re-sewn by a different, finer hand than the rest.
items.hooks: One corner grommet has been re-sewn by a finer hand than sewed the rest, in waxed silk thread no chandler on this coast stocks. The work was done from the inside, with the tent pitched and its flap laced shut.
items.name: Fine Tent (two-person)

dnd5e.mechanics: Shelters two Medium creatures. Pitches or strikes in 1 minute with two sets of hands (5 minutes alone). The taut canvas doesn't flap or snap in wind: occupants sleep through storms without their long rest being disturbed, and at night the silent camp grants advantage on Dexterity (Stealth) checks made to keep the campsite unnoticed by sound.

pf2e.mechanics: Shelters two Medium creatures. 1 minute to set up or strike with two people (5 minutes alone). Occupants resting inside are protected from severe weather, and the silent, non-flapping canvas grants the campsite a +1 circumstance bonus to Stealth checks to avoid being detected by sound.

at_the_table: On the night the storm hits and everyone's shivering, the player who bought this gets to feel very smart.
Fire on demand is quiet power: burning a rope bridge, lighting a signal, cremating something that must not rise.
items.description: A soldered tin with a gasket of oiled leather, holding flint, a hardened steel striker, and char cloth packed like it matters — because it does. The striker throws fat orange sparks even in a wet wind. The lid's interior is polished bright enough to double as a signal mirror in a pinch.
items.hooks: An arsonist has been working the market district, and every witness mentions the same detail: no lantern, no torch, just a figure crouching for a single breath before the flames took. The magistrate is now noting who owns a fine tinderbox — and the party's names may already be on the list.
items.name: Fine Tinderbox

dnd5e.mechanics: Lights a fire as an action even in wind or drizzle (no check required where a standard tinderbox would need one). The sealed tin keeps tinder dry through submersion.

pf2e.mechanics: Ignite a fire in 1 round even in wind or light rain; the sealed tin protects tinder from water.

at_the_table: The gate search where guards pat down every traveler and hand the cloak back without finding the letter.
Three cold, wet nights on the road, and one party member wakes up dry, rested, and insufferable about it.
items.description: Tight-milled wool with a beeswax finish that beads rain into silver drops and sheds them at a shrug. The hem carries lead shot sewn into the seam, so it hangs still in wind that snaps everyone else's coat like a flag. Four flat pockets hide along the inner lining — and the previous set of stitches beside them shows there used to be five.
items.hooks: The tailor who cuts these charges the same price whether you want four pockets or five, but he sews the fifth only when a certain courier house sends the customer. The last cloak he made with five came back for resale within a week, and the fifth pocket had been cut out with a knife.
items.name: Fine Traveling Cloak

dnd5e.mechanics: As traveler's clothes. Rain and wind while wearing it don't make your rest count as sleeping in rough conditions, and its four interior pockets escape a pat-down search unless the searcher succeeds on a DC 15 Intelligence (Investigation) check.

pf2e.mechanics: As traveler's clothing. While worn, exposure to rain and wind doesn't interfere with your rest, and the concealed interior pockets (light Bulk total) require a successful DC 20 Perception check to find; a frisk without Searching gets no check.

at_the_table: In desert or badland arcs where water is the real currency, the fine skin's "doesn't spoil, doesn't burst" line quietly becomes the most valuable gear in the party.
Offering the last clean water in your skin is a scene. Discovering yours was slashed in the night is a bigger one.
items.description: Double-stitched goat hide with a pitch-and-beeswax lining and a carved horn stopper that seats on a leather gasket. Full, it gurgles low and contented; the water inside tastes faintly of wax and nothing else — a small luxury anyone who's drunk from a sour skin will pay for twice.
items.hooks: A caravan outfitter sells fine skins stamped with a running-antelope brand and swears by their lining. Three travelers who bought from the same batch have returned complaining of vivid, identical dreams — of a well, a rope, and something at the bottom asking to be pulled up.
items.name: Fine Waterskin

dnd5e.mechanics: Holds 4 pints. The pitch-sealed lining keeps water cool and clean; contents don't spoil or take on taint from heat, and the skin doesn't leak or burst from a fall.

pf2e.mechanics: Holds 4 pints. Contents stay potable in extreme heat, and the skin isn't damaged by falls or rough handling.

at_the_table: One stool, five tired people: watching who takes it, who offers it, and who it's wordlessly set out for tells the table more than a session of dialogue.
The old soldier who unfolds a stool at the ambush site and sits, calmly, while everyone else crouches in the wet — that's a character established in one object interaction.
items.description: Three ash legs and a triangle of ox hide, scissoring open with a creak you come to find companionable. The hide is polished dark in the middle by years of one particular seat, and someone has notched the leg-tops so the stool always assembles the same way in the dark. It weighs less than the argument over who gets the log.
items.hooks: Guides on the high pass keep a custom: at each night's camp, one stool is unfolded, set at the fire, and left empty. Ask them who it's for and they'll change the subject. Ask them what happens if you sit in it, and they stop talking to you altogether.
items.name: Folding Camp Stool

dnd5e.mechanics: Unfolds or folds with one hand as an object interaction. Supports up to 300 lb. on any reasonably level ground and counts as a dry, stable seat for using tools in camp — mending, scribing, fletching, and cooking proceed without the fumbling of working from a squat in the mud.

pf2e.mechanics: One Interact action to unfold or fold. Supports up to 300 pounds on level ground and serves as a stable, dry work seat, letting you perform Crafting activities such as Repair in the field as though you had a proper place to sit.

at_the_table: The classic that never appears in the equipment chapter of anyone's memory — until the corridor with the too-clean floor. The pole makes trap-probing a declared, visible playstyle instead of a DM negotiation.
Ten feet of reach is also a bridge tester, a depth gauge, a flag mast, and a way to press the suspicious button from around the corner.
items.description: Three sections of straight-grained ash joined by brass ferrules that thread together smooth as a flute. Assembled, it's rigid enough to lean on; broken down, it rides a pack without announcing that its owner walks into places where the floor lies. The tip is capped in iron and dented like a veteran's shield.
items.hooks: The adventurers' guild resells poles recovered from expeditions that didn't return. Guild custom says you carve your name on your pole; the one on the rack right now has four names, each crossed out by the next.
items.name: Folding Ten-Foot Pole

dnd5e.mechanics: Three brass-ferruled ash sections that assemble into a rigid 10-foot pole in one action, or break down to a 4-foot bundle that straps to a pack. Probing ahead with it grants the prodded square's worth of warning: mechanical floor triggers (pits, pressure plates) activate at the pole's end, not underfoot.

pf2e.mechanics: Assembles or collapses with an Interact action. While you Search at half speed probing with the pole, mechanical floor hazards you fail to notice trigger 10 feet ahead of you rather than in your square.

at_the_table: The party doesn't fight past the checkpoint; they hand over papers and hold their breath while the guard reads.
Restocking is its own scene — official paper isn't sold, it's stolen, and every scrivener who supplies it knows exactly what it's for.
items.description: It smells of vinegar, beeswax, and old paper — the smell of a records office with something to hide. Ink bottles are labeled not by color but by institution: customs black, chancery brown, a red the tag identifies only as "tax." Half the wax blanks are pristine; the other half carry test impressions of a seal that has been carefully gouged out of each one.
items.hooks: One burin in the kit is worn to fit a stranger's grip, and the practice sheets rolled beneath the tray repeat a single name in a slowly improving hand. Records at the chancery say the person who owns that name signed a confession last spring. The signature on the confession is the best version on the sheet.
items.name: Forgery Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as a forgery kit: papers of a dozen weights and ages, iron-gall and carbon inks, cut nibs, wax blanks in official colors, and seal-carving burins. Copying a signature from a sample takes 10 minutes; reproducing a seal requires a wax impression of the original or a day carving a blank. Supplies cover roughly a dozen documents before restocking.

pf2e.mechanics: The tools needed to Create a Forgery using Society (or Deception to Impersonate a document's bearer, at the GM's discretion). Contains materials for roughly a dozen documents. Official seals, watermarked stock, or unusual inks may increase the DC until you acquire a genuine sample.

at_the_table: In the jungle arc, the whine at the edge of hearing never stops — except for the characters under net. Who bought netting and who laughed it off becomes the party's health ledger.
One net, drawn over the feverish NPC the party is escorting out, is the pound of gear that decides whether the escort mission has a living client at the end.
items.description: Mesh so fine it reads as mist, folding down to a bundle you can close one fist around, smelling faintly of the citronella oil it was cured in. Against a lamp it shows its weave like a fingerprint, and every veteran of the fever country checks that weave before checking the price. This one has a single darned patch, neat as surgery, right where a sleeper's mouth would be.
items.hooks: A quiet agent in the port is buying every yard of netting at double the asking price and burning none of the usual questions on quality. The weavers are delighted. The fever wards, upriver where the netting should be going, report their shelves emptier every week.
items.name: Insect Netting

dnd5e.mechanics: A fine-mesh net that drapes over one sleeping Medium creature or hangs across a 10-foot space. Creatures fully beneath intact netting rest untroubled by ordinary insects and have advantage on saving throws against diseases transmitted by insect bite. A swarm of insects must spend its turn tearing through the netting — destroying it — before it can reach anyone beneath.

pf2e.mechanics: Fine mesh covering one resting Medium creature, or a 10-foot space when hung. Creatures beneath intact netting gain a +2 circumstance bonus to saves against diseases transmitted by insect bites while resting, and an insect swarm must spend 1 round tearing through the netting (destroying it) before it can affect anyone beneath.

at_the_table: The honest trade of climbing gear: absolute security bought with absolute noise. Ten hammer blows echoing down a dungeon corridor is a wandering-monster invitation the party chooses on purpose.
Fixed ropes turn a one-time obstacle into party infrastructure — a way in and, more importantly, a way *out*.
items.description: Ten square-forged spikes with ring eyes, still smelling of the forge oil they shipped in, rattling together in a canvas roll. The tips are chisel-cut to bite stone. Old climbers can read a cliff face by the rust stains of pitons past — every route ever tried leaves its iron behind.
items.hooks: Halfway up the gorge cliff, a line of pitons marks a route no local guide will claim. They're driven top-down — hammered by someone descending from the plateau above, where nothing is supposed to live.
items.name: Iron Piton Set (10)

dnd5e.mechanics: Ten iron spikes. Hammered into rock or timber, each anchors a rope securely (no check to stay set under one climber's weight). Driving one takes an action and is loud — audible up to 300 feet.

pf2e.mechanics: Ten pitons. Each securely anchors a rope once hammered in (an Interact action); the hammering is audible up to 300 feet.

at_the_table: The party treasury made physical: 25 lb. of shared trust that someone has to carry.
Thieves who can't crack it steal the whole box, which turns a burglary into a chase.
items.description: Riveted iron plate with a rolled lip, a hasp thick as your thumb, and carrying handles that bruise the shoulders of whoever draws the short straw. It's cold in any weather and arrives smelling of the forge. Two keys come with it, and the smith asks — every time — who gets the second one.
items.hooks: A strongbox came up in the harbor dredge last month, still locked, and the moneylender who had reported one stolen paid to have it opened in front of witnesses. It held no coin, no papers, and no water. It held its own second key, and the key was on the inside.
items.name: Iron Strongbox

dnd5e.mechanics: Holds 1 cubic foot or 100 lb. AC 19, 30 hit points, immune to poison and psychic damage. The integral lock opens with a DC 15 Dexterity check using thieves' tools. Sold with two keys.

pf2e.mechanics: Holds 1 cubic foot (4 Bulk of contents). Hardness 9, HP 36, BT 18. Picking the lock requires 3 successes at DC 20. Sold with two keys.

at_the_table: Crossing the marble gallery a half-step at a time, and the rogue looks down to discover the fighter — who left his mail at the inn — is somehow right behind her.
Day six of the overland slog: everyone else is limping and airing blisters at the fire, and one character offers, unbearably, to take the second watch too.
items.description: They smell of neatsfoot oil and nothing else — no new-leather stiffness, no creak when you flex the toe. The cobbler lasted them from a tracing of your bare feet, and the first step feels like the thousandth. Where a heel should click on flagstone, a core of pressed felt lands like a held breath.
items.hooks: The cobbler keeps a carved wooden last of every foot he has ever fitted, shelved and labeled, going back forty years. Last month a stranger paid him to make a pair from one of the old lasts — not their own — and paid triple to take the last with them when they left.
items.name: Masterwork Boots

dnd5e.mechanics: As ordinary footwear, with no breaking-in: they never cause blisters, soreness, or disadvantage related to footwear on a march. While you move at half speed or slower across stone, tile, or board, the felted heel makes no sound of its own — this quiets your footfalls only, not your armor, your gear, or anything you carry. They don't wear out from ordinary use, and the maker's mark holds their resale value.

pf2e.mechanics: As ordinary footwear, comfortable from the first step: footwear never contributes to fatigue from overland travel. While you Sneak across stone, tile, or board, your footfalls make no sound — this quiets your steps only, not your armor or gear, and grants nothing when you move at full Speed. The boots aren't damaged by ordinary wear, and the maker's mark keeps their resale price high.

at_the_table: The difference between "the door groans open" and "the whole floor hears you fail."
Guards who find one on a traveler draw exactly the right conclusion. Owning it is a statement; explaining it is a roleplay scene.
items.description: Forge-folded steel with a wedge tip ground thin enough to slip a warded lock plate, and a shepherd's-crook heel that bites without slipping. The balance is uncanny — it hangs in the hand like a weapon that chose a trade. Somewhere near the grip, the smith struck a tiny mark.
items.hooks: Only one smith in the region strikes that grip-mark, and she sells exclusively to people she's vetted personally. If the party didn't buy theirs from her, she'll want to know — politely, at first — where they got it.
items.name: Masterwork Crowbar

dnd5e.mechanics: Grants advantage on Strength checks where leverage applies (as a crowbar) and doesn't bend, chip, or lose function on a failed check. Counts as a club in a pinch.

pf2e.mechanics: As a crowbar, and you don't take the –2 item penalty to Force Open without one; the bar is never damaged by a critical failure to Force Open.

at_the_table: A locked box the rogue can't speed-pick mid-scene turns "loot it" into "carry it out, and decide who studies it tonight."
Buying one is an interview. The maker builds each lock's sequence personally, and remembers every client — and every box.
items.description: A dark walnut case bound in blued steel, faced with a dial of interlocking brass petals where a keyhole ought to be. The petals turn with a watchmaker's smoothness and no sound at all. Under the lid's lip, stamped small, is the maker's mark: an open eye.
items.hooks: Whoever commissions an open-eye lockbox trusts its maker with the one fact that matters: he can open every box he's ever built, blind, in seconds. Three of his clients have died in the past year. All three boxes were found open, and nothing official was reported missing.
items.name: Masterwork Lockbox

dnd5e.mechanics: Holds half a cubic foot. AC 19, 25 hit points. The puzzle-lock has no keyhole: opening it unaided requires a successful DC 15 Intelligence (Investigation) check to learn the sequence, then a DC 20 Dexterity check using thieves' tools. Its maker can open it blind. Knock and similar magic work normally — and the lid chimes loudly when they do.

pf2e.mechanics: Holds half a cubic foot (2 Bulk). Hardness 9, HP 30, BT 15. The puzzle-lock requires a successful DC 20 check to Decipher Writing (or Crafting) to learn the sequence before it can be Picked: 5 successes at DC 30. The maker can open it in a single Interact action.

at_the_table: Three days from the nearest forge, the paladin's breastplate is split down a seam. With these, the fix made by firelight is the fix that finishes the campaign.
Armorers quote different prices once they see the mark come out of the pack. Some of those prices go down.
items.description: The hammer settles into your grip as if it took a measurement first, and the tongs close with a click you feel more than hear. Every face is dressed mirror-bright except the strike surfaces, which carry the honest gray of work. Each piece bears the same stamped anvil-and-star, and older smiths touch the mark before they touch the tool.
items.hooks: The anvil-and-star was a teaching mark: a master granted it to journeymen who surpassed her, and she granted it nine times. Guild records list eight sets of these tools. Whoever carries the ninth set either earned it from a woman twenty years dead, or took it from someone who did.
items.name: Masterwork Smith's Tools

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as smith's tools. You have advantage on checks to repair metal objects, armor, or vehicles in the field, and a repair made with them holds — it doesn't reopen, loosen, or fail under ordinary use. The tools themselves never chip, warp, or break.

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as artisan's tools (blacksmithing) with a +1 item bonus to Crafting checks to Repair metal items. A critical failure to Repair with them doesn't deal damage to the item, and the tools can't be broken through normal use.

at_the_table: The party's face walks past the ball's doorkeeper on posture and brocade while the rest queue at the servants' entrance with the wine barrels.
Wearing it into the wrong quarter of the city is a decision; every cutpurse on the street does the arithmetic at a glance.
items.description: Brocade with real metal thread — you feel the weight of it settle on your shoulders like a hand of approval. It rustles expensively when you move and carries a ghost of ambergris that outlasts three launderings. The buttons are carved bone, and the second-from-top has been replaced by a lesser hand, the way ransomed clothing often is.
items.hooks: A replaced button reads to a court tailor the way a mended hoof reads to a farrier: whoever owned this was stripped of it once and got it back. Three suits out of the same estate sale this season carry the same lesser hand's repair, in the same place, second from the top. The family has never reported a robbery, a ransom, or a death.
items.name: Noble Attire

dnd5e.mechanics: As fine clothes. While worn, doorkeepers, servants, and functionaries presume you belong: you have advantage on Charisma (Persuasion) checks to gain entry or service anywhere admission is judged by dress. You are also a marked target — Dexterity (Sleight of Hand) checks to pick your pockets are made with advantage.

pf2e.mechanics: As fine clothing (high-fashion). While worn, you gain a +1 circumstance bonus to Make an Impression and Request checks against those who judge status by dress, and doorkeepers admit you without challenge where dress determines entry. Thieves mark you: creatures gain a +1 circumstance bonus to Steal from you in a crowd.

at_the_table: Two coppers of wood buys the sweetest sound in dungeoneering: something heavy hitting a door that stays shut. Wedges turn "run!" into a fighting retreat with punctuation.
Wedging a door *open* is the quieter genius move — no clang of a closing portcullis-trap, no sealed tomb behind you.
items.description: Four blunt teeth of seasoned oak, kick-scarred and dark with boot polish and dungeon grime. The grain is dense enough to shrug off a shoulder charge, and the taper is cut for stone thresholds, not parlor floors. They knock together in the pouch like dice — the sound of a party that plans its exits.
items.hooks: The carpenter carves a fifth wedge free for regulars, and hers carry a small maker's mark. One just turned up on the *inside* of a vault door in the magistrate's building — wedged by someone who wanted to make very sure nothing followed them out.
items.name: Oak Door Wedges (set of 4)

dnd5e.mechanics: Four hardwood wedges. Kicked under a door (an action), one holds it shut or open: forcing a wedged door requires a DC 15 Strength check, or DC 17 with two wedges. Removing your own wedge is a free interaction.

pf2e.mechanics: Four wedges. Setting one under a door is an Interact action; a wedged door requires a Force Open check against a DC of 17 (or 19 with two wedges) in addition to any lock.

at_the_table: The most double-booked pint in the game: every flask spent as a weapon is six hours of light the party no longer has. Make the ledger visible and the choice gets delicious.
A poured line of oil is battlefield authorship — players redrawing the map before the fight starts.
items.description: A squat clay flask stoppered with wax-dipped cork, heavy with rendered fish oil or pressed seed oil depending on what the region has to spare. It sloshes with a low gulp when handled, and everything it touches carries the smell for a day. Chandlers chalk the fill date on the base — old oil burns dirty.
items.hooks: Someone bought the chandler's entire stock this morning — forty flasks, paid in old coin, loaded onto a cart heading toward the granary district. The chandler mentions it only because the buyer never asked the price.
items.name: Oil Flask (1 pint)

dnd5e.mechanics: Fuels a lantern for 6 hours. As per the SRD, it can instead be thrown (range 20/60) to coat a target — igniting the oil deals 5 fire damage — or poured to cover a 5-foot square that burns for 2 rounds when lit.

pf2e.mechanics: Fuels a lantern for 6 hours, or functions as the oil item: thrown or poured and ignited for persistent fire damage per the core rules.

at_the_table: Hour six of cold rain: the party's morale splits cleanly along the line of who spent the 3 gp at the last port.
The one thing an oilskin can't do is sneak — crossing the wet deck unheard means taking it off, and taking it off means the rain wins.
items.description: Stiff canvas boiled in wax and linseed, the color of dark honey, smelling like a chandler's back room in summer. New, it stands up on its own and crackles like a fire when you bend an elbow; a season of wear teaches it your shape. Rain hits the shoulders and runs off in ropes, drumming a sound you'll learn to sleep through.
items.hooks: The chandler rewaxes old sets cheap and resells them, and nobody minds; oilskins outlive their owners. The set she sold you has a name inked inside the collar, half boiled away. She'll tell you it came off a wreck last winter — but the wreck she names lost no one, and the name in your collar isn't on any crew list she'll show you.
items.name: Oilskin Set

dnd5e.mechanics: Waxed coat, leggings, and sou'wester hat. While worn, rain and spray don't soak you or anything carried beneath the coat — tinder stays dry, paper survives, and a night of rain doesn't make your rest count as sleeping in rough conditions. The wax coat is loud: Dexterity (Stealth) checks while moving in it are made with disadvantage.

pf2e.mechanics: Waxed coat, leggings, and brimmed hat. While worn, you and items carried beneath the coat stay dry in rain and spray, and rain doesn't interfere with your rest. The stiff waxed cloth creaks and crackles: you take a –2 circumstance penalty to Stealth checks to Sneak while wearing it.

at_the_table: The answer to "we take *all* of it": the statue, the wine, the fourth body's share. Someone straps in, and the party's pace becomes a decision.
A loaded frame can't run. Choosing who carries it on the way out of hostile country is choosing who the party will not leave behind.
items.description: Steam-bent ash lashed with rawhide, worn smooth wherever it meets shoulder and hip. The frame creaks in a slow rhythm as you walk — a sound porters call "the song" and stop hearing after the first mile. Hash marks burned along one upright count somebody's finished jobs.
items.hooks: A porter's frame turned up at a mountain waystation with sixty-one burned hash marks and its load still lashed on — food, oilskins, and a strongbox nobody's opened. Porters won't touch it. The sixty-first mark is only half burned in.
items.name: Pack Frame

dnd5e.mechanics: A rigid frame worn like a pack. Your carrying capacity increases by 50 lb. for gear lashed to the frame, but while loaded past your normal capacity you have disadvantage on Dexterity (Acrobatics) checks and can't take the Dash action.

pf2e.mechanics: Increases the Bulk you can carry before becoming encumbered by 2. While carrying more than your normal limit, you take a –10-foot penalty to all Speeds (this doesn't stack with the encumbered penalty).

at_the_table: The alchemist stops asking the party to wait in town. Every campsite becomes a workshop, and every workshop becomes a smell the whole camp votes on.
Setting up the rig at an inn draws a crowd, a constable, or a customer — sometimes all three, in that order.
items.description: Folded shut, it could pass for a courier's chest; open, it blooms into a bench — copper burner, nested retorts sleeved in wool, a rack of stoppered reagents that clink like distant bells when the mule stumbles. It smells of sulfur, mint, and scorched cork, and no amount of airing changes that. Someone has riveted a small silver plaque inside the lid and then, later, pried the name off it.
items.hooks: A small silver plaque was riveted inside this rig's lid, and someone later worked the name off it with a blade. The rivets stayed. Count them: nine, in two rows — and no workshop in the trade sets a nameplate with more than four.
items.name: Portable Alchemy Rig

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as alchemist's supplies. You can craft alchemical items while traveling, making crafting progress on any day you travel or camp at half the normal daily rate. The rig packs or unpacks in 10 minutes and survives rough transport without breakage.

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as alchemist's tools. You can Craft alchemical items during downtime spent traveling, counting each travel day as half a day of work. Setting up or breaking down the rig is 10 minutes of Interact actions, and the glassware is cradled against damage from ordinary travel.

at_the_table: Burying a fallen companion properly, days from any temple, is the scene this item exists for. The ten minutes of setup is the party standing in silence, and the table will stand with them.
An oath sworn at the shrine binds harder in the fiction than any contract: the players saw the candles lit.
items.description: Three hinged panels of close-grained wood, dark with decades of incense, that open with the resinous breath of every prayer said inside them. The carving is left deliberately unfinished at the center panel — blank, so any god's sign can be set there — and wax from other travelers' candles has pooled in the sconces in four different colors. It folds to the size of a book of sermons and weighs about as much.
items.hooks: The pilgrim selling this one swears it was blessed at a mountain sanctuary and carried a single holy circuit, hence the price. But the sconces hold sixteen layers of wax, the hinge pins have been replaced twice, and the blank center panel isn't blank — it's been carved and planed smooth again, more than once.
items.name: Portable Shrine

dnd5e.mechanics: A folding wooden triptych with candle sconces, incense drawer, and an amulet holy symbol that serves as a spellcasting focus. Unfolding and consecrating the shrine takes 10 minutes and sanctifies a 10-foot space until the shrine is struck: rites, oaths, funerals, and any ceremony requiring an altar or consecrated ground can be performed there.

pf2e.mechanics: A folding triptych with sconces, incense drawer, and a religious symbol usable as a divine focus. Setting up takes 10 minutes and dedicates a 10-foot space until the shrine is packed away; the space counts as a consecrated site or altar for rituals, rites, and ceremonies that require one.

at_the_table: The chase turns a corner; the watch pounds past a bored tradesman in gray who was, eight seconds ago, a fleeing merchant in blue.
Wearing it to a meeting says something to anyone who recognizes the work: this person plans exits.
items.description: Heavier than it looks, because it's two coats sharing one set of seams: scuffed gray laborer's wool on one face, merchant's broadcloth with horn buttons on the other. The turn is fast — the tailor set every buttonhole to work from both sides, a trick that takes as long to sew as the rest of the coat combined. Only the collar betrays it, if someone thinks to fold the collar back.
items.hooks: Fold the collar back and the tailor's chalk is still on the inner seam: two numbers, the second one higher than the first. Coats like this are cut two to a bolt and numbered as a pair, so the twin of the party's coat is out there, wearing somebody. Last week a witness swore she saw that same blue broadcloth on both sides of the river within the hour.
items.name: Reversible Coat

dnd5e.mechanics: As traveler's clothes. Turning the coat takes an action and changes its color, cut, and apparent station — drab laborer's wool one way, respectable merchant's broadcloth the other. A witness describing you by your clothing must succeed on a DC 15 Wisdom (Perception) check to connect the two outfits; pursuers working from the old description don't recognize you by dress.

pf2e.mechanics: As traveler's clothing. Reversing the coat is a 3-action activity (a single Interact action if someone assists) and swaps its color, cut, and apparent station. You gain a +2 circumstance bonus to Impersonate checks made only to avoid being recognized as the person seen in the other configuration.

at_the_table: Bulk logistics made cheap: water for the desert crossing, oil for the siege, or the pickled proof of what's been eating the livestock, carried home to someone who can identify it.
Found sealed in a ruin, a jar is a small mystery with a built-in dramatic beat: the ribbon of wax, the pause, the smell.
items.description: Fired river clay with a comfortable heft and a glaze that crazes into fine spiderwebs after a season's use. The wax seal peels up in one satisfying ribbon, and the smell underneath tells you immediately whether you're glad you opened it. Potters scratch their initials into the base while the clay is wet.
items.hooks: A farmstead's cellar holds forty jars, all sealed by the same hand, all scratched with the same initials — and the family that lives there now can't say whose they are. They've been eating from the jars all winter. The seals at the back of the cellar are newer than the ones at the front.
items.name: Sealed Clay Jars (set of four)

dnd5e.mechanics: Each jar holds 1 gallon. Wax-sealed contents keep for a season and survive full submersion; a sealed jar with airspace floats. AC 11, 1 hit point — they shatter, not dent.

pf2e.mechanics: Each jar holds 1 gallon. Sealed contents are protected from water and spoilage for three months. A jar is fragile: any damage breaks it.

at_the_table: The party is two days from anywhere, the pursuit is one day behind, and the fighter's left sole flaps like a broken jaw.
A character who kneels to check a hireling's boots before a long march is doing quiet, memorable leadership.
items.description: The leather smells of the tanning shortcut that made it cheap, and the heels are stacked paper board under a skin of hide. New, they gleam with a blacking that rubs off on your thumb. The soles are pegged, not stitched — count the pegs and you can guess the week they'll start walking away from the uppers.
items.hooks: A garrison quartermaster took the low bid and shod three hundred soldiers in these before the autumn campaign. He knows what he bought — he's been selling the good boots out the back gate, and the cobbler who threatened to tell the captain hasn't opened her shop in nine days.
items.name: Shoddy Boots

dnd5e.mechanics: As ordinary footwear. At the end of any day you travel at a fast pace or undertake a forced march, roll a d6; on a 1–2 a sole splits, and until repaired (1 sp and an hour at a cobbler) you have disadvantage on saving throws against exhaustion from marching and your travel pace can't exceed normal.

pf2e.mechanics: As ordinary footwear. After any day of overland travel beyond 8 hours or at increased Speed, attempt a DC 5 flat check; on a failure a sole splits, giving you a –5-foot penalty to Speed during overland travel until the boots are repaired (Repair, or 1 sp at a cobbler).

at_the_table: It costs less than a night at a good inn, and it works right up until the moment it matters most. Sell the discount; collect the drama.
A character digging through it mid-crisis learns exactly what the price bought — and who they saved that gold for.
items.description: The buckles are mismatched and the leather has the sour, cellar smell of damp that was dried out in a hurry. Half the loops are empty, the salve tin rattles, and one bandage roll unwinds to reveal a rust-brown stain someone rolled to the inside. The previous owner's initials have been scraped off the lid — not sanded, scraped.
items.hooks: The stained bandage roll was wound with the mark turned inward, which is a habit you pick up in a field hospital and nowhere else. The initials on the lid weren't sanded away, they were scraped — with the edge of the salve tin that's still rattling in the case. Whoever did it worked in a hurry, and worked one-handed.
items.name: Shoddy Healer's Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: Counts as a healer's kit, but only 6 of its nominal 10 uses remain intact. When you expend a use, roll a d6; on a 1, that dressing is spoiled and the use is wasted (the creature isn't stabilized until you expend another).

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as healer's tools with roughly half their supplies missing. Each time you Administer First Aid or Treat Wounds, attempt a DC 5 flat check first; on a failure, the materials you draw are spoiled and you take a –2 item penalty to that Medicine check.

at_the_table: Doubles the party's oil budget and adds a flinch to every stumble — dungeon tension bought at a discount.
The light leak around the hood means "hooded" is optimistic: sharp-eyed sentries may still catch the glow.
items.description: Dented tin with a warped hood that never quite seats, leaking a wobbling halo of light around its seams. The handle's solder joint flexes when it swings. It smells of old fish oil because that's mostly what it's been fed.
items.hooks: The pawnbroker's shelf holds six of these, all the same make, all pawned in the same week by the same crew of miners. The mine claims the crew quit. The lanterns say nobody planned to.
items.name: Shoddy Hooded Lantern

dnd5e.mechanics: As a hooded lantern, but burns oil at twice the rate, and any hard jolt (a fall, a hit, rough handling) risks guttering the flame — DC 10 Dexterity check to steady it or it goes out.

pf2e.mechanics: As a hooded lantern, but burns oil twice as fast; on any critical failure while it's carried in hand, the flame gutters out.

at_the_table: The cheap option players choose in a hurry, and the tense re-read of this file when someone's dangling from it.
Merchants sometimes coil shoddy rope under a fine top layer; a passed appraisal or inspection catches the splices.
items.description: Loose-laid hemp with visible splices where shorter offcuts were married together. It smells faintly of the harbor it was salvaged from, and dry fibers dust off in your grip. Coiled tight, it looks fine — which is exactly the problem.
items.hooks: A porter's guild has been quietly buying shoddy rope in bulk and reselling it as new to a rival mining camp. The first broken hauler was called an accident. The second wasn't called anything — nobody's found him.
items.name: Shoddy Rope (50 ft.)

dnd5e.mechanics: As hempen rope, but on a climbing or securing check that fails by 5 or more, the rope frays or snaps. AC 11, 1 hit point.

pf2e.mechanics: As rope, but treat any critical failure while it bears weight as also severing the rope.

at_the_table: The looting montage goes fine. The sprint back to the boat, sacks bouncing, is when you find out what a running stitch is worth.
A spilled sack is a map: guards, rivals, or something hungry can follow the trail of dropped coin and candlesticks straight to the party.
items.description: Coarse burlap that sheds fibers on everything it touches, sewn with a single loose running stitch and a knot at each end. Held to the light, the weave shows daylight through it. The bundle smells of the granary floor it was swept from.
items.hooks: The ragpicker sews these from sacking the granaries sell off cheap, and this month's bundle came out of the low quarter's oldest store-house. Every sack in it carries the same brown stain across the bottom seam — the same shape, the same height on all five, as though the whole stack stood a long while in one shallow pool.
items.name: Shoddy Sacks (bundle of five)

dnd5e.mechanics: As a sack (30 lb. capacity). Whenever one carries more than 15 lb. through a chase, climb, or forced march, roll a d6 at the end of the scene: on a 1, a seam gives and the contents spill behind you.

pf2e.mechanics: As a sack. If it holds more than 2 Bulk, any critical failure on a check made while hauling it (or a critically failed Athletics check to Climb or Swim) also splits a seam, spilling the contents.

at_the_table: The first drip lands at three in the morning, on the character with the lowest patience, and the party discovers exactly who they are when they're wet and it's nobody's fault.
The price gap between this and a real tent is a character decision: the veteran pays it without being asked, and everyone notices who doesn't.
items.description: Loose-weave canvas that smells of mildew before it has ever been rained on, patched with whatever the last owner had — a flour sack, a horse blanket, one square of good oilcloth that only makes the rest look worse. Pitched dry it looks almost respectable. The seams are the sales pitch and the confession in one.
items.hooks: Every tent from the merchant's current bale carries the same charcoal mark inside the ridge seam — a circle with a line through it. He says it's a warehouse tally. The soldiers who sold him the bale marked their dead the same way.
items.name: Shoddy Tent (two-person)

dnd5e.mechanics: Shelters two Medium creatures — in dry weather. On any night of rain or snow, the seams let go: each occupant must succeed on a DC 10 Constitution saving throw to gain the benefits of their long rest, and the soaked canvas weighs an extra 8 lb. until it spends a full day drying.

pf2e.mechanics: Shelters two Medium creatures in fair weather. During rain or snow, the tent leaks: each occupant must succeed at a DC 14 Fortitude save or be fatigued the following day, and the sodden canvas counts as 1 additional Bulk until it dries over a full day.

at_the_table: Splitting the party stops being a mistake and becomes a plan: the scouts crest the ridge, and everyone at the table watches for the flash.
Smoke on the horizon is a question the players ask themselves — ours, theirs, or someone in trouble who saw our column first?
Anything beyond the agreed signals needs a code both ends have learned, and learning one is its own scene: who teaches it, who writes it down, and who kept a copy.
items.description: A flat tin case that rattles faintly with the whistle inside, its mirror polished to a coin-bright disc that flares painfully when the lid opens sunward. The flags smell of dye and campfires, and the smoke-cloth squares are dense, waxy, and heavier than they look. A code card pasted inside the lid has been amended in three different hands, each correcting the last.
items.hooks: For six nights running, a hill above the trade road has flashed the same sequence at dusk — a distress call in a garrison code retired twenty years ago. The garrison that used it was never disbanded on any list. It was recorded lost, all hands, in the hills it's now signaling from.
items.name: Signal Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: A steel signal mirror, two colored flags, a signal whistle, and three squares of smoke-cloth. In clear conditions, mirror flashes read at 10 miles, flag code at 2 miles, and a burning square of smoke-cloth at 5 miles (it burns 1 minute). Sending a prearranged signal takes 1 minute.

pf2e.mechanics: Steel mirror, paired flags, signal whistle, and three squares of smoke-cloth. In clear conditions, mirror flashes read at 10 miles, flag code at 2 miles, and a burning square of smoke-cloth at 5 miles (1 Interact action to light, 1 minute of colored smoke). Sending a prearranged signal takes 1 minute.

at_the_table: "How deep is it?" becomes a ritual with a payoff: the cord goes down, the table goes quiet, and the tallow comes up holding the answer — wet sand, rust flakes, hair.
The cord that goes taut *early*, or comes up bitten clean, is a whole encounter announced in one prop.
items.description: Sailor's gear gone underground: a hundred feet of tight-laid cord knotted at every tenth foot, ending in a lead plummet with a cup of soft tallow set into its base. Drop it and count the knots through your fingers in the dark. What sticks to the tallow when it comes back up is the floor of the pit, delivered for inspection.
items.hooks: Quarrymen sounded the flooded lower gallery last month and the plummet returned with fresh candle wax in the tallow — from a passage sixty feet underwater, in a mine that's been sealed for a generation.
items.name: Sounding Cord (100 ft.)

dnd5e.mechanics: A knotted cord with a lead weight, marked every 10 feet. Lowering it measures the depth of pits, wells, and chasms up to 100 feet, and reads the bottom: the weight's tallow-packed base brings up traces of what it lands on (water, sand, bone, nothing).

pf2e.mechanics: A weighted, knotted 100-foot cord marked every 10 feet. An Interact action per 20 feet lowered measures depth; the tallow-packed weight retrieves traces of the surface it touches.

at_the_table: The party bought light by the copper and the dungeon knows it: half-hour timers, a sputtering d6 at the worst moments, and a smoke trail any pursuer can follow.
Five bad torches invite the classic gambit — burn them as decoys, thrown lures, or a false camp while the real party moves in darkness.
items.description: Green pine batons wrapped in rag and dipped in whatever the renderer had left at the bottom of the vat. They light easily, spit sparks constantly, and weep black smoke that clings to the ceiling — and the lungs. The peddler ties them in fives with a straw cord and calls them "traveler's bundles," cheerfully declining to travel with them himself.
items.hooks: The rag wrapping on this batch is shredded livery — the colors of a noble house that dissolved a decade ago. Somebody is emptying that estate one wagon-load at a time, and burning the evidence by the bundle, two coppers a sale.
items.name: Sputter Torches (bundle of 5)

dnd5e.mechanics: As torches, but each burns for only 30 minutes, and in wind, rain, or after a hard knock, roll a d6: on a 1, the torch dies and won't relight. Sold in bundles of five.

pf2e.mechanics: As torches with a 30-minute duration; in wind or rain, or when the bearer critically fails a check, the torch gutters out and can't be relit. Bundle of five.

at_the_table: The scout's answer to "who opens the door?" — nobody, yet. Corners, ledges, and murder-holes get checked with one wrist instead of one head.
A mirror also reads as the party's monster-lore paying off: some things you check for reflections *on purpose*, and the table knows exactly why.
items.description: A palm-sized oval of polished steel riveted to a jointed brass handle that folds like a heron's leg. The reflection is honest but dim — faces in it look like memories of faces. The back is stamped with the polisher's proof mark and a spider web of scratches from every corner it has peered around.
items.hooks: The guild sells these mirrors used, and this one has a habit the polisher can't buff out: in one specific corridor of the old sewer works, it shows the corner ahead — and a tall figure standing in it that isn't there when you look directly.
items.name: Steel Inspection Mirror

dnd5e.mechanics: A polished steel mirror on a jointed 2-foot handle. Lets you see around corners, under doors, and over ledges without exposing yourself; you can make Perception checks on areas the mirror can reflect while remaining in cover.

pf2e.mechanics: A mirror on a jointed 2-foot handle. You can Seek areas the mirror can reflect (around corners, under doors) while remaining behind cover.

at_the_table: Two farmers, one creek that moved, and a party the whole village watches walk the line: a boundary dispute is a duel where the weapon is arithmetic.
Measure the villain's manor against its floor plan, and the study is eight feet shorter than it should be.
items.description: The chain pours out of its sack link by cold link, each one stamped with a guild assay mark, and the ranging rods still smell of the red paint on their tips. The plumb bob is brass, heart-shaped, and polished by a century of pockets. Chalked on the inside of the case lid is a sum — two parcels, an acreage, and a difference — that somebody underlined three times.
items.hooks: Surveyors in this region carry a bonded license, because a chain-length of error moves fortunes. The widow selling this kit kept her husband's field books, and the last one runs out mid-page: a line of chain measurements that leaves the parcel he was hired to survey and keeps going east, four more pages, across land nobody owns.
items.name: Surveyor's Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: A measuring chain, ranging rods, plumb line, and sighting level. With 10 minutes of work you can determine exact distances, areas, and elevations without a check. Comparing your measurements against deeds, plans, or memory grants a DC 10 Intelligence (Investigation) check to expose discrepancies — moved boundary stones, hidden rooms, a building shorter than its floors add up to.

pf2e.mechanics: With 10 minutes of measuring, you establish exact distances, areas, and elevations without a check. Checking those figures against deeds or building plans lets you attempt a DC 10 Society or Crafting check to detect discrepancies such as shifted boundary markers or concealed spaces.

at_the_table: The lantern hinge, the crossbow trigger, the snapped clasp on the map case: nothing in the pack stays broken, provided the party can spare an evening.
Mending a stranger's kettle at a shared fire buys more honest gossip than a round of drinks.
items.description: A canvas roll gone soft and dark at the fold lines, smelling of solder, beeswax, and machine oil. Inside wait small pliers, files worn to their last honest teeth, a spirit lamp, wire in three gauges, and a tobacco tin of scavenged screws — no two alike. A tally of hatch marks runs along the inner flap, well past a hundred, one for every thing brought back from the dead.
items.hooks: What did the roll's last owner fix, out there, that was worth a hatch mark deeper and darker than all the rest? The tinker who sold it won't guess, but she'll point out that the mark isn't scratched in like the others. It's burned.
items.name: Tinker's Roll

dnd5e.mechanics: A traveling subset of tinker's tools (which cost 50 gp in full): counts as tinker's tools for repairing objects of Small size or less, but each repair takes twice the usual time, and the roll can't be used to craft new items.

pf2e.mechanics: Counts as a repair kit. You can Repair only items of 1 Bulk or less, and each attempt to Repair takes 10 minutes with the roll's limited tools. It lacks the materials to Craft new items.

at_the_table: The countdown clock of every wilderness arc. Counting remaining wraps is tension no monster can match.
Sharing rations with a starving stranger is the oldest trust scene in the genre. It still works.
items.description: Twice-baked biscuit hard enough to knock on, a fist of salted meat, dried fruit leather, and a knot of smoked cheese, all wrapped in waxed cloth. What's actually in the wrap varies by region — river towns pack smoked fish, hill country packs mutton — and travelers can taste where their supplier bought stock.
items.hooks: The provisioner's latest batch all came from one estate sale, and the fruit leather carries a faint taste of bitter almonds. Nobody's died — yet — but the town's hounds refuse to touch the stuff.
items.name: Trail Rations (1 day)

dnd5e.mechanics: Feeds one Medium creature for one day. Keeps for two months; after that, each day's ration carries a risk of spoilage (DC 10 Constitution save or be poisoned for 1 hour).

pf2e.mechanics: Feeds one Medium creature for one day. Keeps for two months; spoiled rations require a DC 14 Fortitude save to avoid being sickened 1.

at_the_table: The statue is too heavy, the chest is too heavy, the fighter is too heavy — and the travois turns "we can't" into "we can, at half speed, leaving a track a blind man could follow."
Dragging a wounded companion out over two days of bad country, pole-ends scoring the earth behind you, is the slowest and best kind of victory lap.
items.description: A bundle of oiled straps and woven webbing that looks like nothing until it meets two straight poles — then it becomes the shape every hunter and stretcher-bearer knows at a glance. The leather is stained dark at the shoulder loops where it rides against a working body for miles, and one strap has been chewed through and knotted back together by someone in a hurry.
items.hooks: A hunter found travois tracks on the high trail: two clean pole-lines and boot prints, heading up the mountain, weighted going in. There is no returning track, no camp, and no season in living memory when anyone hauled a loaded travois toward the peak. The pole-lines stop at a rock face, mid-stride.
items.name: Travois Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: Straps, lashings, and a webbed bed that rig two poles (included, or cut fresh in 10 minutes) into a drag-sled. Assembly takes 10 minutes. A creature dragging the travois moves at half speed and can haul up to 300 lb. of cargo on it, or one Medium creature. A stabilized or unconscious creature can be moved on it without further harm from jostling.

pf2e.mechanics: Rigging that turns two poles (included, or cut on-site in 10 minutes) into a drag-sled; assembly takes 10 minutes. While dragging it your Speeds are halved. The bed holds up to 8 Bulk or one Medium creature, and a stabilized dying or unconscious creature can be transported without being harmed by the movement.

at_the_table: Attending the funeral of someone the party got killed, faces hidden in plain sight, while the family receives condolences three feet away.
The etiquette shield: the guard captain has questions, but pulling a veil from a mourner's face in public is a line even he hesitates to cross.
items.description: The veil weighs nothing — a black net that turns your face into a suggestion while leaving the room sharp to your own eyes. The kid gloves fit close as a second skin and smell faintly of lavender water, the way gloves do when they're kept in a drawer with letters. The world treats a veiled figure with a hush; people lower their voices around grief without deciding to.
items.hooks: The milliner keeps a customer book, and one entry troubles her enough to mention it: a woman has bought the same veil-and-glove set on the first market day of every month for a year. Never a word about why, always the lavender gloves in the same size — and last month, for the first time, the size changed.
items.name: Veil and Gloves

dnd5e.mechanics: A face veil of fine dark net and close-fitted kid gloves. While worn, your face, hands, and any marks on them can't be seen: checks made to recognize or identify you by appearance are made with disadvantage. Where mourning dress is customary, wearing the set invites no questions — and pressing a veiled mourner with them is itself a breach of manners.

pf2e.mechanics: A net veil and kid gloves. While worn, they conceal your face, hands, and identifying marks, granting a +2 circumstance bonus to Impersonate checks made only to conceal your identity. In communities where veiling or mourning dress is customary, wearing the set draws no suspicion by itself.

at_the_table: The reason the treasure map survives the river crossing — or the reason the villain's correspondence is still legible when looted from a body in the rain.
A sealed case invites the question every table loves: do we open someone else's mail?
items.description: A leather tube dipped in beeswax until it shines like old amber, capped at both ends with cork-lined lids that close with a satisfying thock. It smells of honey and lamp smoke. Scratches in the wax record every journey it's survived.
items.hooks: Couriers of a certain trading house wax their cases in a distinctive red. One such case has been sitting unclaimed at a crossroads inn for three weeks, and the innkeeper has started offering coin to anyone willing to deliver it — no questions answered.
items.name: Waxed Map Case

dnd5e.mechanics: Holds up to ten rolled sheets of paper or five of parchment. Contents stay dry through rain and full submersion of up to 1 minute.

pf2e.mechanics: Holds ten rolled sheets. Contents are protected from water as if in a sealed container; brief submersion doesn't damage them.

at_the_table: The pass is snowed in, the shortcut over the ridge saves four days, and the whole question is: who bought the kit and who said they'd be fine.
Removing a mitten to work a lock, string a bow, or feel for a pulse — with the cold counting the seconds.
items.description: It arrives as one dense roll that smells of cedar shavings and animal fat, heavier than any single garment has a right to be. The coat's fur faces inward, hide out, and the hood is cut deep enough to turn your face into a warm cave. Someone has already worn the mittens long enough to shape them — the furrier calls this "proofing," and doesn't say who does it.
items.hooks: The furrier's stock is better this season than anyone can remember — deep pelts, whole hides, no trap scars. He buys from a valley three days north where, the drovers mention, the trapping families stopped coming to market in the spring. The pelts keep coming down anyway.
items.name: Winter Kit

dnd5e.mechanics: A bundled set: fur-lined coat and hood, mittens over wool liners, felted boot socks, and a wax-treated scarf. While the full kit is worn, you have advantage on saving throws against exhaustion caused by extreme cold weather. Fine manipulation with the mittens on requires a free hand or removing one (an object interaction).

pf2e.mechanics: Bundled cold-weather clothing: coat, hood, mittens, liners, and felt socks. While the full kit is worn, you're protected against severe environmental cold as if properly outfitted, and you gain a +1 circumstance bonus to Fortitude saves against extreme cold. Mittened hands can't perform fine Interact tasks without pulling one off.

at_the_table: Wearing it means asking somebody to read your own name off your ribs. That is a scene, and it happens once per owner.
The names come and go, so the armor is a rotating cast the DM can deal from: whoever surfaced this month is somebody the party can now go and find, or bury.
items.description: Half plate in dark, close-fitted steel, the breast dented twice and never dressed out. Names surface in the metal the way frost surfaces on glass — thin bright letters that rise over a few days, hold for a season, and sink away again. They are the names of everyone who has worn it. Yours arrives about a week in, low on the left side, under the arm, where you cannot read it without help.
items.hooks: Sixty-one names have been recorded off this armor by the garrisons that have held it, and the lists don't match. Four names appear on every list. Nine appear once and never again. And one name has surfaced in every single season since the records begin, in the same place on the right pauldron, belonging to a woman who by every account never wore the armor at all — she commissioned it.
items.name: Armor of the Fallen Watch, +1 Half Plate

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 bonus to AC. Base armor: half plate.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 half plate.

at_the_table: Pursuit stops working, which means the DM has to chase the party with something other than a tracker — and the party feels clever for a whole session.
The displaced prints are the price. Somewhere, someone is finding the party's footprints in places that make no sense, and drawing conclusions.
items.description: Low, soft-soled boots in oxblood leather with a hooked toe, comfortable from the first mile. Behind you the ground closes over itself — snow smooths, mud fills, dust settles — and you can turn and watch it happen at the edge of the light. Your prints do get made. They surface somewhere else: a mile off, a day later, a clear line of your tread crossing a field you have never walked.
items.hooks: A hunting lodge has been logging a trespasser for two years: the same tread, always crossing the same three fields, never entering or leaving them, no prints at the boundaries. They have staked out the fields eleven times. Last spring the line of prints crossed a field on the far side of a river the tread never touched.
items.name: Boots of the Quiet Mile

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement. While worn, you leave no tracks, scent trail, or disturbance for anyone to follow — snow, mud, dust, and wet stone all close behind you. Creatures tracking you by physical sign find nothing; magical or divinatory tracking is unaffected.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested. While worn, you leave no tracks, scent, or physical trace; creatures attempting to Track you by physical sign find nothing. Magical or divinatory tracking is unaffected.

at_the_table: Carrying capacity stops being the constraint, which frees a party to haul the statue, the evidence, and the fourth share — and gives the DM permission to hand them something enormous.
The rummage is the joke and the tension both: the round spent finding the right vial is a round the satchel chose to cost them.
items.description: A plain canvas dispatch bag with a bone toggle, no deeper inside than out, and it takes whatever you put in it. What it will not do is keep things where you left them: reach in for the rope and find it under the spare boots, which are under a lantern that was on top an hour ago. Everything is always there. Nothing is ever where you last had it.
items.hooks: Sold as a courier's bag, and couriers won't have them — a satchel that reorders itself can't be sworn to in front of a magistrate. This one came from a chandlery clearance with a length of chain still buckled through the toggle and a customs seal on the chain, unbroken, from a port that stopped issuing that seal a long time ago.
items.name: Bottomless Satchel

dnd5e.mechanics: The satchel holds up to 200 lb. or 8 cubic feet, and always weighs 3 lb. regardless of contents. Retrieving a specific item takes an action. Turning it inside out or overfilling it spills the contents; nothing is destroyed.

pf2e.mechanics: The satchel holds up to 20 Bulk and always counts as 1 Bulk regardless of contents. Retrieving a specific item is a single Interact action. Overfilling or inverting it spills the contents without destroying them.

at_the_table: One character walks the whole miserable journey dry, and the party's feelings about that are the actual content of several evenings.
The debt is the design. Somewhere ahead is a night where four days of held-off storm arrive at once, on one person, and the DM gets to pick when.
items.description: A weighty traveling cloak in undyed wool with a deep hood, and under it the light is wrong in a way that takes a day to notice: always the flat gold of an hour before sunset, at noon, at dawn, under a black storm sky. Rain arrives at your shoulder and goes around. Snow reaches the wool and is somewhere else. The hem is never wet, and never dusty, and never anything.
items.hooks: Cloaks like this are sold with the debt disclosed, and buyers take them anyway. A carter on the northern run wore one for nine years and never paid, which the trade regards as impossible and the carter regarded as luck. He has retired to a house with no windows on the weather side, and he still won't sleep through a storm.
items.name: Cloak of Small Weather

dnd5e.mechanics: While worn, the weather within arm's reach of you is fair and mild whatever the sky is doing: rain parts, snow doesn't settle, heat and cold ease to a pleasant day. It shelters you alone, offers no protection against magical weather or damage, and the weather it turns aside arrives on you later — at a time the DM chooses, in full, once per journey.

pf2e.mechanics: While worn, the weather within arm's reach is fair and mild regardless of conditions, sheltering you alone. It gives no protection against magical weather or damage, and the weather it holds off returns on the wearer in full once per journey, at a time the GM chooses.

at_the_table: Six hours to a flask of oil, and this ends the accounting forever — which quietly rewrites every dungeon budget the party has ever made.
The off-true shadows are a free plot sensor. Somewhere there is a room where they fall correctly, and the player who notices will not stop talking about it.
items.description: Brass gone soft-gold with handling, with a wick that never shortens over a reservoir that has never once needed filling. The flame sits perfectly still — no flicker, no lean toward a draft — and throws a light a shade whiter than fire has any business being. Watch the shadows it casts and you'll find they fall a few degrees off from where they ought to, as though the lamp were standing slightly to the left of where you set it.
items.hooks: The chandlers' guild in three cities has petitioned to have these declared contraband, and each petition is withdrawn a season later without a hearing. The lamp the party is carrying has a guild seal struck into its base, filed down but not filed away. It was shop inventory once, in a shop that no longer sells lamps.
items.name: Everburning Lamp

dnd5e.mechanics: Sheds bright light in a 15-foot radius and dim light for an additional 15 feet, as a hooded lantern. It needs no fuel and can't be put out by wind or water; closing the hood is the only way to darken it.

pf2e.mechanics: Sheds bright light in a 20-foot radius (dim light to 40 feet). It requires no fuel and isn't extinguished by wind or immersion; only the hood shutters it.

at_the_table: Strapped across a sleeper's back on a cold watch, it does a bedroll's work — and the character who lends it out is making a visible choice.
Walking it into a building tells the party something before anyone rolls: it is warmest where a household is, and it does not care whether that household is friendly.
items.description: A round shield of limewood faced in boiled hide, its boss dented flat on one side, and it is warm — always, on both faces, the low steady warmth of a stone that has sat near a fire. Carry it into a house and it warms further, until under a roof with people in it you can feel it through a gambeson. Out on open ground it goes down to blood heat and stays there.
items.hooks: The shield was the door-guard of a longhouse for six generations, hung on the inside wall and taken down twice. The family that owned it is scattered and its youngest is a cooper two towns over, who does not want it back and will not say the word "sold" aloud. She will, however, tell you the exact spot on the wall where it hung, and how the boss came to be flat.
items.name: Hearthguard, +1 Shield

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 bonus to AC beyond the shield's normal bonus while wielded.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 sturdy shield (Hardness 5, HP 20, BT 10).

at_the_table: One direction, forever. The party's navigation problems become navigation *choices*: they always know where home is, and that's a different pressure than being lost.
Buying one secondhand means buying somebody else's destination. The needle won't tell you whose — only where.
items.description: A palm-sized brass case under a glass face, with a needle of dull iron — and it weighs what a full waterskin weighs, a difference you feel the instant someone hands it to you. The needle holds its bearing so steadily that it looks painted onto the card. Turn the case in your hand and the needle turns with the world instead of with you.
items.hooks: Every secondhand compass points somewhere, so buying one is inheriting a stranger's unfinished business. This one has a name scratched inside the lid in a hand that ran out of room halfway through. Its needle points at no city on the coast, but at a stretch of open water eleven miles out, where every chart in the port agrees there is nothing at all.
items.name: Homing Compass

dnd5e.mechanics: The first time the compass is held while someone who has stood in a place names it aloud, the needle turns to that place and never turns anywhere else. It points true through fog, darkness, and stone, and gives direction only — never distance, never a route. The naming can't be undone.

pf2e.mechanics: The first time the compass is held while someone who has stood in a place names it aloud, the needle fixes on that place permanently. It points true through fog, darkness, and stone, giving direction only — never distance or route. The naming can't be undone.

at_the_table: A contract, a confession, a will: a page in this ink that survived the night was *meant*. That's a fact the party can carry into a courtroom or to a graveside.
The player who writes a letter in it and finds it blank by morning has learned something the DM never had to narrate.
items.description: A squat bottle of ink so black it reads as a hole cut in the page, and it never entirely dries — run a thumb across a line written a decade ago and it will still smudge, faintly, and mark your skin. Writing with it feels ordinary right up until you set the pen down, at which point you already know whether the words are going to keep. Scribes describe that moment as being told something about yourself you hadn't asked about.
items.hooks: Chanceries won't accept documents in it and lovers swear by it, which tells you most of what you need to know. A magistrate three towns over keeps one page of it framed behind her bench, forty years old and unfaded: a confession to a killing, signed by a man her court acquitted. She hung it at the height where every defendant has to read it.
items.name: Ink of Second Thoughts

dnd5e.mechanics: Anything written in this ink fades to nothing within a day — unless the writer meant it without reservation as they wrote, in which case it never fades. The writer knows which it was the moment the pen leaves the page. One bottle writes about thirty pages.

pf2e.mechanics: Writing in this ink fades within a day unless the writer meant it without reservation, in which case it never fades. The writer knows which it was as the pen leaves the page. One bottle writes about thirty pages.

at_the_table: Every place the party has ever been welcomed is now a place they can return to at three in the morning. That reframes hospitality permanently, and players feel it.
It rewards note-taking of the best kind: "did we open that door?" becomes the most important question in a heist.
