items.description: A split iron ring hung with keys of every pattern — warded, lever, a flat brass thing for a cabinet, one carved from bone. Count them and you get a number; count them again and you get one more. The extra key is never the same key twice, and it is never the one you need, and it is always warm from a pocket.
items.hooks: The ring's power is a record of hospitality abused, which is why guild locksmiths cut a new pattern rather than sell one on. A house on the hill has had its locks changed four times this year, at ruinous cost, by an owner who cannot explain to the smith what he is protecting against. He has begun asking whether a door that is bricked up still counts as a door.
items.name: Keyring of Familiar Doors

dnd5e.mechanics: Any door, gate, or lid the holder has opened before — by key, by picking, or by permission — can be opened by the ring again, unlocked with a touch and an action. It has no effect on a door the holder has never opened, and none on a door that has since been walled up or replaced.

pf2e.mechanics: Any door, gate, or lid the holder has previously opened can be unlocked with a touch (1 Interact action). It has no effect on doors the holder has never opened, or on doors since replaced or sealed shut.

at_the_table: One hour, one room, once a day. That is a tight enough leash that the party has to guess *which* room matters, and being wrong costs them the day.
What it shows is silent and partial, so it generates arguments rather than answers. The table will spend twenty minutes on what a figure in a doorway was carrying.
items.description: A squat iron lantern with a horn shutter and no fuel port anywhere on it. Lit, it throws an ordinary orange working light. Opened all the way, the light goes the color of weak tea and the glass turns cold enough to ache against a bare palm — cold that lasts exactly as long as the hour it is showing you.
items.hooks: An assize court leased one for a season and stopped, and the clerk's note on the return gives the reason in one line: the lantern had begun showing the room an hour ago *and* a second, fainter room over the top of it, which nobody could place. The two rooms shared a door in the same wall. The court's chamber has no door in that wall.
items.name: Lantern of Last Hours

dnd5e.mechanics: Once per day, open the shutter fully in an enclosed space and wait 1 minute. Everyone present sees the room silently as it stood one hour ago, held for 1 minute — figures, objects, and positions, with no sound and no detail the room itself didn't hold. It shows the room, not the people: faces are clear only if they were lit.

pf2e.mechanics: Once per day, open the shutter in an enclosed space and wait 1 minute. All present silently see the room as it was one hour earlier, for 1 minute — positions and objects only, no sound, and faces legible only where the room was lit.

at_the_table: The best kind of unreliable narrator is an object. Rustle the mail when the party is safe and they will believe the room is dangerous; rustle it never, and they'll believe the opposite.
A DM who wants the shiver to mean something specific should decide privately and never confirm it. Half the value is the argument at the table.
items.description: Fine riveted mail, oiled black, light enough over the shoulders that you keep checking it's still there. Every so often the rings shiver — a fast dry rustle across the chest and down one side, like rain starting on a roof — and then stop. It does this in barracks and on empty roads, before nothing and before everything, and no two veterans who have worn it agree on what it means.
items.hooks: The shirt came off a wall-watch that was cut down to a man, and that man walked eleven miles to report it before he sat down and did not get up. It has been reissued four times since, always to someone standing a watch, and the garrison list beside its serial number has one column filled in and one left blank. The blank column is headed *returned*.
items.name: Last-Watch Mail, +1 Chain Shirt

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 bonus to AC. Base armor: chain shirt.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 chain shirt.

at_the_table: Every haggling scene now has a referee. That doesn't end the negotiation; it moves it to what the merchant is willing to admit in front of a book.
Courts and tax assessors want it far more than merchants do. Owning one openly is a political position.
items.description: A ruled merchant's daybook in a scuffed board cover, half its pages already filled. New lines arrive in ink that never matches the color of the line above, in a clerk's hand that changes with the region — round and generous in the river towns, cramped and slanted in the hills — as though the book keeps hiring locally.
items.hooks: A guild bought a ledger like this eleven years ago to audit its own warehouses, and the audit is still running, because the book keeps writing lines for goods nobody has laid on it. The entries are all for the same warehouse and all for the same weight of the same spice, once a month, at a value that has fallen by half over the decade. That warehouse burned down in the second year.
items.name: Ledger of Honest Weight

dnd5e.mechanics: Lay goods on the open ledger, or the ledger on them. Within a minute a line writes itself giving the true quantity, quality, and fair market value of what it touched, in local coin. It reports value, not history — it can't tell you a thing is stolen, cursed, or counterfeit-by-story, only what it actually is and what it's actually worth.

pf2e.mechanics: Place goods on the open ledger, or the ledger on them; within a minute a line writes itself stating true quantity, quality, and fair local market value. It reports what a thing is and is worth, not its history — it doesn't detect theft, curses, or forged provenance.

at_the_table: Witnesses are the real security system in any city, and this removes them. The party can commit a crime in front of forty people and walk past the same forty tomorrow.
The limit is the good part: friends still know you. Every betrayal this mask enables has to be done to strangers.
items.description: A soft half-mask of undyed kid leather, so light on the face that within a minute you stop feeling the edges of it. The outside is blank and takes no expression. The inside is worn into hollows — brow, cheek, the bridge of a nose — in the shape of a face that is not yours and will not be, however long you wear it.
items.hooks: Watch captains know the pattern before they know the object — a month of thefts, dozens of witnesses, and not one usable description. One captain has a drawer of forty statements from a single robbery, all of them agreeing on the coat, the height, and the voice, and all forty leaving the face blank. She has started interviewing people about hands.
items.name: Mask of Plain Faces

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement. While worn, you look entirely ordinary — not disguised, not hidden. Creatures see you normally and can point you out in the moment, but afterward can't recall or describe your face, and can't identify you from a likeness. Anyone who knew you before the mask recognizes you as they always did.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested. While worn, you appear unremarkable rather than disguised. Creatures perceive you normally at the time but afterward can't recall or describe your face or identify you from a likeness. Creatures who already knew you recognize you normally.

at_the_table: The party's kit stops degrading, and the fighter's cloak slowly becomes a history of perfect seams over ruined wool.
Somebody will stay up to watch it. That scene is the whole reason the item exists, and it should always end with them falling asleep.
items.description: A slim steel needle blued almost to black, with an eye so small that no thread anyone owns will pass through it. Set it down on torn cloth at night and by morning the tear is gone, closed in stitching finer than the garment ever deserved. Sit up and watch it, though, and it lies there being a needle — it has never once moved while anyone was looking, and every owner has tried.
items.hooks: Tailors' guilds forbid apprentices to own one, on the grounds that a needle which sews unwatched teaches nothing. This one came out of a master tailor's estate, her tools sold off in a separate lot to a separate buyer. The inventory doesn't list the needle among the tools. It lists it with her jewelry.
items.name: Mending Needle

dnd5e.mechanics: Leave the needle overnight with one torn or worn item of cloth, leather, canvas, or rope; by morning it is whole. One item per night. It has no effect on metal, wood, stone, or flesh.

pf2e.mechanics: Leave the needle overnight with one damaged cloth, leather, canvas, or rope item; by morning it is fully Repaired with no check. One item per night. It has no effect on metal, wood, stone, or flesh.

at_the_table: Knowledge without enforcement is the cruelest possible design, and players understand it instantly: you will know, you will not be able to prove it, and you will not be able to stop it.
Give the second band to an NPC and the party has a live wire running out of the campaign into someone else's life.
items.description: Two plain bands of soft red gold, sized to no particular finger and comfortable on any. Worn, a band draws in a fraction — a small deliberate tightening you feel below the knuckle — whenever the other wearer says your name aloud, wherever they are. Long-paired wearers stop noticing it the way you stop noticing a heartbeat, and notice immediately when a day goes by without one.
items.hooks: Bands are made in pairs and buried in pairs, and a single band on the market means one of two things. This one came in from an estate with its twin listed on the same inventory line, struck through in a different ink. The seller can produce the inventory, the strike-through, and a receipt. He cannot produce the twin, and the band he is selling has been tightening, on and off, all week.
items.name: Oathkeeper Bands (pair)

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement, and only works as a pair worn by two attuned wearers. When either wearer breaks a promise made aloud while both wore the bands, both know it happened at the moment it happens — the fact only, not the terms, the reason, or where. It compels nothing and prevents nothing.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested; functions only as a pair worn by two investing wearers. When either breaks a promise made aloud while both wore the bands, both immediately know it has happened — the fact alone, with no detail and no compulsion.

at_the_table: Split the party across a city, a siege line, or a plane and they still hold one channel: *rung, twice, now*. Agreeing on what the counts mean is a five-minute scene that pays out for a campaign.
Whoever holds the twin holds a claim on you. Giving one away is a promise, and being given one is a leash you agreed to wear.
items.description: Two thumb-sized bells of dark bronze on separate cords, and neither one has a clapper — turn them over, shake them, hold them to the light, and there is nothing inside to make a sound with. Squeeze the body of one and the other rings, wherever it is, in whoever's hand. The bronze is worn brightest at the place a thumb goes.
items.hooks: Bells are made in pairs and separated constantly — by death, by falling-out, by pawnbrokers who only ever get the one. The bell on this counter has rung four times since it came in: twice the week it arrived, once a month after that, and once yesterday afternoon. The pawnbroker has taken it out of the window.
items.name: Quiet Bells (pair)

dnd5e.mechanics: Sold as a pair. Squeezing one bell is silent to everyone except whoever carries its twin, who hears it clearly at any distance on the same plane. It carries no words — only that it rang, and how many times.

pf2e.mechanics: Sold as a pair. Squeezing one bell is silent to all but the bearer of its twin, who hears it clearly at any distance on the same plane. It conveys no words, only the fact of the ring and the count.

at_the_table: A player who fills this with an NPC's face has told the table who their character is without writing a word of backstory.
Grief with a mechanism: the likeness doesn't fade, which means the owner never gets the mercy of forgetting what they looked like.
items.description: A flat silver oval worn thin at the hinge, holding a miniature so fine it stops reading as paint. Look at it directly and it's a good likeness and no better — a competent court painter's work. Catch it at the edge of your vision while you're doing something else and it is exactly them, the whole face, moving the way you'd see it across a crowded room, and every owner learns not to do that on purpose.
items.hooks: Lockets outlive the people inside them, and no pawnbroker can open one — that's the entire design. A collector buys them sealed at a fair price and has two hundred now, none of which he can open. He buys more every year. The shelf he keeps them on is arranged by year of purchase, with one gap left near the middle.
items.name: Rememberer's Locket

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement. Hold the locket closed against one living face for 1 minute to fix that likeness inside it. From then on only you can open it, and the likeness never fades, ages, or alters. One locket holds one face.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested. Hold the locket closed against one living face for 1 minute to fix that likeness inside it. Thereafter only the investing owner can open it, and the likeness never fades, ages, or alters. One locket holds one face.

at_the_table: Real-time correspondence across any distance changes what a split party can attempt. It also means the DM can deliver bad news mid-scene, one letter at a time.
Watching the other person hesitate is the whole item. A sentence begun, erased, and replaced tells the party more than the sentence does.
items.description: Two hand-sized tablets of dark slate in wooden frames, each with a stub of chalk on a string. Words arrive stroke by stroke as the other hand makes them, which means you watch your correspondent hesitate, cross out, and start again. Ink and chalk both dry at a normal pace on ordinary news and slow to a crawl on bad — a line about a death can stay wet for an hour, and every long-term user knows what a slow-drying slate means before they read it.
items.hooks: Slates are sold in pairs and a pair outlives its owners, which is why courier offices buy up singles and hold them. One office keeps a shelf of nineteen unpaired slates under a cloth, and about once a season one of them writes something. The staff have standing instructions to copy down whatever appears, wipe the slate, and never write back. The book of copied lines is nearly full.
items.name: Speaking Slates (pair)

dnd5e.mechanics: Sold as a pair. Anything written on one slate appears on the other at the same moment, in the writer's own hand, at any distance on the same plane. A slate holds about fifty words; wiping either one clears both.

pf2e.mechanics: Sold as a pair. Writing on one slate appears simultaneously on the other in the writer's hand, at any distance on the same plane. Each holds about fifty words, and wiping either clears both.

at_the_table: The quirk is a free plot sensor: the party's dagger "smells stronger" in a room where the floor was mopped this morning.
Collectors pay a premium for named, quirked weapons over anonymous +1s — which makes selling it a negotiation rather than a transaction.
items.description: An unremarkable blade with a walnut grip, worn pale where a thumb rides — until it's drawn, when the air around it fills with the warm brown smell of cinnamon. The scent is strongest in the first moment of the draw and fades as the blade stays out, so a fight smells of it once and then not at all. Near the recently dead it doesn't fade.
items.hooks: Spicebiter has changed hands eleven times, and its previous owners share one detail: not one of them sold it. Each swears it was stolen, or that they woke and it was gone from a locked room. The dealer who has it now sleeps with it under the counter, and has begun leaving the counter unlocked.
items.name: Spicebiter, +1 Dagger

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: dagger.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking dagger.

at_the_table: Inventory stops being an argument. The cord remembers what the party counted three weeks and one head injury ago.
The count that doesn't match is the adventure: eleven knots, ten crates. Somebody counted honestly, and somebody moved something.
items.description: Four feet of undyed hemp, soft as an old bootlace, that knots itself along its length as you count aloud — you feel each knot draw tight against your palm a half-beat after you say the number. Left hanging on a peg, it creaks: the slow working creak of a rope with weight on it, though nothing hangs from it and nothing ever has. Quartermasters keep theirs in a drawer for that reason.
items.hooks: A harbor clerk's cord went in as evidence last spring and the case came apart around it — sixty-two knots against a manifest of sixty. The clerk swore he had counted true, and the cord agreed with him, because the cord only ever agrees with the counter. Two crates came off that ship that nobody has found since, and the cord is still knotted, in a box, in a magistrate's cupboard.
items.name: Tally-Cord

dnd5e.mechanics: Name what you're counting and the cord knots itself, one knot per item, as you count. It holds that count indefinitely and can't be untied by anyone but the counter. It records only what its holder actually counted — it doesn't perceive, search, or verify.

pf2e.mechanics: Name what you're counting and the cord ties one knot per item as you count. The count persists indefinitely and only the counter can untie it. It records what its holder counted and nothing else — it doesn't perceive, search, or verify.

at_the_table: A weapon that leaves permanent, recognizable marks means the party's history walks around on other people. Someone will come back with a scar and a good memory.
It makes no one bleed out, which is quietly humane and quietly horrible: the blade is the interrogator's weapon of choice for exactly that reason, and everyone knows it.
items.description: A short leaf-shaped blade, grey and matte, that takes no shine however it is worked. Wounds it makes do not bleed — the edges part, stay parted, and show clean and dry down to whatever is underneath. They also do not close: a cut from this blade knits no faster than the flesh around it decides to, and healed ones stay visible as pale open-looking seams for the rest of a life.
items.hooks: There are perhaps forty people alive with the seams, and they find each other — there is a word for it in two languages and a house in the capital where they drink for free. None of them agree on how many blades there are. What they agree on is that the marks are all identical, all the same width, and that two of them were made in the same room on the same night three hundred miles apart.
items.name: The Bloodless Blade, +2 Shortsword

dnd5e.mechanics: +2 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: shortsword.

pf2e.mechanics: +2 greater striking shortsword.

at_the_table: The player's own initials appear. Nothing else in the game makes ownership feel like that, and nothing else makes selling an item feel like a decision with a witness.
Every pair on the head is an NPC the DM can invent on demand, in order, with a built-in reason the party wants to find them.
items.description: A working hatchet with a hickory haft and a poll scarred from use as a hammer, and the flat of the head is crowded with initials. They arrive on their own, small and neat, a new pair within a day of a new owner taking it up — and they cannot be removed. Filed, ground, or heated, they come back by morning in the same hand, in the same place in the sequence, which is why the head now has to be read in a spiral.
items.hooks: Count the initials and you get sixty-one pairs. Ask after the axe in any village along the river road and someone will name it as stolen goods, describe a different theft, and be telling the truth. The most recent pair on the head is not the party's yet — it belongs to someone still alive, who has been looking for eleven years, and who will recognize the spiral before they recognize a face.
items.name: The Borrowed Axe, +1 Handaxe

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: handaxe.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking hatchet.

at_the_table: The party's high ground becomes an asset with a price tag. Every tower, every summit, every ride on something with wings is now worth climbing for the map alone.
The fading is the campaign clock. A five-year-old chart is nearly gone, so the Eye rewards parties who go back and look again — and punishes the ones who thought they were finished.
items.description: A flat brass case the size of a prayer book, holding a single sheet of vellum that is never used up. Lines arrive on it in a fine brown ink while you watch, unhurried, the way frost crosses a window. What it draws does not keep: a coastline mapped this spring is already yellowed and soft-edged by autumn, and a river you charted five years ago is a ghost of itself, faded as though the sheet has been out in a hundred years of sun.
items.hooks: The Eye has mapped one particular valley eleven times for eleven owners, and the guild that holds those copies has them side by side under glass. Ten of them agree. The eleventh is the oldest, the most faded, and the only one drawn before the road went through — and it shows the valley with a lake in it, where the ten newer sheets show a town.
items.name: The Cartographer's Eye

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement. Any terrain you have seen from above — a summit, a tower, a flying mount — draws itself onto the blank vellum inside the case, accurate and to scale, within an hour of your seeing it. It maps ground only: no creatures, no interiors, nothing under a roof.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested. Terrain you have seen from above draws itself onto the case's blank vellum, to scale, within an hour of your seeing it. It maps open ground only — no creatures, no interiors, nothing roofed.

at_the_table: The mace is a clock the player carries. Every peaceful session it gets heavier, and the moment they finally swing it is the moment the campaign's tension breaks.
A character who won't use it and won't sell it is telling you something. Let them carry it up a mountain.
items.description: A short flanged mace with a leather-wrapped haft and a head the color of old pewter, and it gains weight the longer it sits. A week on a peg and it drags at the belt; a month and you notice it on the stairs; left in a chest for a season it takes two hands to lift out. Use it once and it comes back to a comfortable four pounds in the space of a breath, as though it had been waiting to be asked.
items.hooks: Moneylenders in three cities recognize the flanging and will lend against it sight unseen, at a rate that is generous to the point of rudeness. Every one of them asks the same question before handing over the coin, in the same flat way, as though reading it from a card: *how long since you last used it?*
items.name: The Debtor's Mace, +1 Mace

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: mace.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking mace.

at_the_table: Every body of water on the map becomes a place with a history the party can read. Harbors, wells, flooded galleries, and the ford where the caravan was lost all have something on the bottom.
What it shows is where things *came to rest*, not where they went in. The gap between those two facts is most of a mystery.
items.description: A ship's lantern in pitted bronze, its glass clouded to the color of a winter sky, heavier than bronze accounts for. The flame inside makes a sound — held close, it is the small continuous hiss of rain falling on a river, a long way off, and it does not change whether the lantern is lit in a dry cellar or forty feet down.
items.hooks: Salvage crews on this coast bid against each other for a week's hire of a drowned lantern, and one crew has bid every year for nine years and never worked a wreck. They take it to the same stretch of open water, hold it down on a line for one night, and bring it up. They pay in advance, they return it clean, and the youngest of them has started asking the older ones what they are counting.
items.name: The Drowned Lantern

dnd5e.mechanics: Burns underwater and in any airless place, shedding bright light in a 30-foot radius. Underwater, its light also shows what the water has taken: objects and bodies lost beneath it appear where they came to rest, visible but not solid, for as long as the light is on them.

pf2e.mechanics: Burns underwater and in airless places, shedding bright light in a 30-foot radius. Underwater it also reveals what the water has claimed — lost objects and bodies appear insubstantially where they came to rest, while the light holds them.

at_the_table: Ammunition stops being a ledger line and starts being a slow, strange mail service: every shot the party takes will come back to them eventually.
The arrow that comes back before it should — same day, wrong direction, wrong mud — is an encounter with no monster in it yet.
items.description: A tall yew bow, back and belly darkened to the color of strong tea, with a nock carved into the shape of a hooded bird's head. Arrows loosed from it are always found again — in the grass, in the mud, in the river, days later and a valley over, but always found, and always by the person who loosed them. Fletchers who have handled it say the arrows come back with their own fletching intact and somebody else's mud on them.
items.hooks: The bow is named for a falconer who is said to have loosed one arrow at something over a lake and then waited on that shore for nine years. There is a shingle beach where a hut used to be and the local children still turn up arrows there, all one fletching, all pointing inland. The count is somewhere past four hundred.
items.name: The Falconer's Longbow, +1 Longbow

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: longbow.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking longbow.

at_the_table: The party cannot turn it off. Every scene requiring darkness, concealment, or a quiet approach now has to route around one member's cargo, and leaving it behind is its own decision.
Its light does not end, so anything that needs the dark must come at it another way. That reframes a whole campaign's worth of enemies.
items.description: A crude thing: a clay bowl, a bronze handle riveted on by somebody in a hurry, and a wick of twisted flax that has never shortened. It is older than the technique used to make it. It smells of the first rain falling on hot stone, and it smells of that in dry seasons, in sealed rooms, and underground — a smell people recognize before they have any idea why.
items.hooks: A city grew around where this lantern was set down, and grew in rings, and the oldest ring is the one whose streets all face the same point. It has been out of that city for two hundred years and the city has not gone dark. Whatever is burning in the shrine at the center is burning without a wick, and the keepers change the oil weekly, and the oil is never gone.
items.name: The First Lantern

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement. Sheds bright light in a 60-foot radius and dim light for 60 feet beyond, and cannot be extinguished, shuttered, dimmed, or hidden by any means while attuned. Its light is not dispelled and does not end; while it burns, magical darkness within its bright light fails.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested. Sheds bright light in a 60-foot radius and dim light 60 feet beyond, and cannot be extinguished, shuttered, or concealed while invested. Its light can't be dispelled or suppressed, and magical darkness fails within its bright light.

at_the_table: The spear frosting mid-conversation is the cheapest suspense the DM owns: every player at the table will decide it means something, and they will decide different things.
Hand it to a superstitious NPC and watch them read their own fortune into a piece of wet ash wood.
items.description: An ash-hafted spear with a leaf blade and a collar of blued iron, and the haft frosts. Not in cold — in high summer, in a shuttered room, in the middle of a crowded hall, a white bloom of rime creeps up eight or ten inches of the wood and stands there for a minute or two before going to water. It has done this on battlefields and at breakfast, and nobody has ever made the pattern mean anything.
items.hooks: The spear turns up in three separate assize records as evidence, always in the same role: it stood in the corner of a room while someone was questioned, and in all three the accused confessed. The clerks note the frost each time, in the margin, in a shorthand they clearly expected the next clerk to understand. Two of the three confessions were later found to be false.
items.name: The Frostmarked Spear, +1 Spear

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: spear.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking spear.

at_the_table: One object that ends every disguise in the campaign is a scalpel, not a hammer: the party has to get the suspect in front of it, which is an entire heist.
It shows and does not dispel. Knowing the ambassador's true shape while everyone else sees the ambassador is the worst possible position, and the best possible session.
items.description: A standing glass in a plain black frame, taller than a person, and it is exactly blood-warm to the touch at every hour and in every weather — a wall of glass that feels like a held hand. What it gives back is not flattering and not cruel. It is only accurate, which people find they were not prepared for, and the room it stands in is always quieter than the room next door.
items.hooks: The mirror has been owned by four courts and each of them stopped using it within a year, for reasons the inventories record as *disuse*. It is currently crated, face-in, in a collector's store-room, and the collector has never had it uncrated. He bought it after seeing it once, at a reception, at a distance, across a crowded floor — and what he says he saw was the room reflected correctly with one person too many in it.
items.name: The Honest Mirror

dnd5e.mechanics: A creature reflected in the mirror is shown as others actually see it: illusions, disguises, shapechanging, and magical concealment all fail in the reflection, which shows the true form beneath. It reveals only — it dispels nothing, and the creature remains disguised to everyone not looking at the glass.

pf2e.mechanics: A creature reflected in the mirror appears as it truly is: illusions, disguises, polymorph, and magical concealment fail in the reflection. It reveals without dispelling — the creature remains disguised to anyone not looking at the glass.

at_the_table: The cloak turns the overland slog into a non-problem, which is exactly what a party wants — until the session where they need to describe the village they walked through six days ago.
Let the player choose what they lose, or don't. Both versions are good, and they are different games.
items.description: Undyed road-wool, patched at both elbows by different hands in different decades, and it smells of nothing at all — not wool, not smoke, not the miles. Wearing it, distance stops accumulating in your legs. What it takes instead is small and specific: at the end of every journey, one place you passed through is gone from you entirely. Not dimmed. Gone, with the shape of it left behind, so you know the size of what you're missing.
items.hooks: Its owners are easy to identify in the records because they all kept journals, obsessively, from the day they put it on. The last owner's journal runs to four volumes and is meticulous about inns, fords, and prices — and it has eleven pages cut out of it with a knife, at intervals of roughly a year. She cut them herself. The stubs are annotated, in her hand: *not this one either.*
items.name: The Long Road Cloak

dnd5e.mechanics: Requires attunement. While worn on an overland journey, you travel as though the distance were half what it is for purposes of fatigue and exhaustion — you arrive rested from a march that ruins everyone else. It doesn't increase your speed or shorten the journey; only what the journey costs you.

pf2e.mechanics: Invested. On an overland journey, you accrue fatigue as though the distance travelled were halved, arriving rested from marches that exhaust your companions. It doesn't increase Speed or shorten travel time — only its cost to you.

at_the_table: The key is a plot generator that runs on its own schedule. Wherever it points next is a place the party has been, which means the DM gets to reopen a location the players thought they were done with.
The best sessions are the ones where it chooses badly: the key that now opens a friend's front door, or a cell the party once got out of.
items.description: A long key in white metal, plain in the bow and elaborate in the bit, and it is a little longer every time you look — not enough to measure against itself, but measure it against a doorframe you know and the difference is there. The reshaping happens overnight and leaves the bit warm and slightly out of true, so the first turn of a morning always catches once before it gives.
items.hooks: Keys like this are the reason certain families change their locks on a fixed schedule for reasons they no longer remember. This one's previous owner kept a list of every lock it ever chose — forty-one of them, in eleven years, in his own careful hand. The last entry is not a lock. It is a date, three weeks in the future from when he wrote it, and he wrote it in the same column as the others.
items.name: The Patient Key

dnd5e.mechanics: The key fits exactly one lock at a time, and opens it perfectly and silently, as often as you like. Once that lock has been opened and closed again, the key reshapes itself overnight to fit a different lock of its own choosing — somewhere you have been. You don't choose the new lock and can't refuse it.

pf2e.mechanics: The key fits one lock at a time and opens it perfectly and silently, without a check. Once that lock has been opened and closed, the key reshapes overnight to fit a different lock of its own choosing, somewhere you have been. The choice isn't yours and can't be declined.

at_the_table: Free compass rose, no mechanics required: the party can note the lean in every room they sleep in and start drawing lines on a map themselves.
The staff propped in the corner of an inn, leaning, is a background detail players will bring up eleven sessions later.
items.description: Blackthorn worn to a shine, shod in iron at the foot and cut for someone a hand taller than most. Stand it against any wall, in any building, on any ground, and it leans — never falling, never straightening, always tipping a few degrees toward the same quarter of the horizon. It isn't downhill, it isn't north, and it isn't toward water. It has been the same direction for as long as anyone has kept track.
items.hooks: Three pilgrim houses keep records of staves like this and the entries are always the same shape: a name, a direction, and a year the walking stopped. This staff's owner is recorded as having walked its lean for six years and then turned around. She got home, lived a long time, and left instructions that the staff be sold to a stranger rather than kept in the family.
items.name: The Pilgrim's Staff, +1 Quarterstaff

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: quarterstaff.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking staff.

at_the_table: The customs shed, the sealed vault, the coffin at the crossroads: the party can now know before they open, which turns "should we?" into a much better question than "can we?"
It doesn't say if a thing is alive. Reading "one man, one lantern, forty pounds of chain" off a sealed crate is a complete scene with no monster in it.
items.description: A counting-frame of nine wires and ninety beads in a hardwood case, small enough to work one-handed. The beads are worn — deeply, unevenly, to the shape of thumbs — but the wear is on the wrong ones: the beads a counter's hand actually falls on are smooth and new, and the polished hollows sit in a sequence nobody has ever managed to reproduce.
items.hooks: Harbor authorities in two cities have tried to buy this outright and been refused by a seller who does not appear to want money. What he wants, according to the clerk who handled both approaches, is a written undertaking that the tally will never be used on the cargo of a particular company — and both authorities refused that, and he kept the tally, and the company has not shipped anything through either port since.
items.name: The Quartermaster's Tally

dnd5e.mechanics: Touch the tally to any closed container — chest, crate, strongbox, coffin — and you know its contents as a list: what is in it and how much, by name and count. It reports contents, not condition, not danger, and not whether anything is alive. It works once per container per day.

pf2e.mechanics: Touch the tally to a closed container to learn its contents as a list of names and counts. It reports contents only — not condition, danger, or whether anything within lives. Once per container per day.

at_the_table: A duel where half the noise is missing puts every spectator on edge, and the DM never has to explain why.
Drawing it in a dark room is the whole trick: the other side hears nothing, and the party knows it.
items.description: A slim court blade with a swept guard and a grip bound in black silk, and it makes no sound. Not a muffled sound — none: it leaves the scabbard silently, it takes a parry silently, and steel that strikes it rings alone, one voice where there should be two. Fencing halls find this harder to be around than they expect, and most masters will only spar against it once.
items.hooks: The blade is named for a killing that happened at a crowded supper table without anyone at it looking up. Four guests gave statements and all four described the same thing: a conversation that stopped, and started again, and the man at the end of the table had not moved for some minutes. Nobody has ever explained what the other three heard that made them turn around at last.
items.name: The Quiet Argument, +1 Rapier

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: rapier.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking rapier.

at_the_table: A minute of climbing rope is a minute of standing in the open, which turns a solved problem back into a scene.
It anchors to the *nearest* thing. Half the fun is the party watching it lash itself to the wrong beam and having to decide whether that's good enough.
items.description: Fifty feet of ordinary-looking hemp, a little furred with age, coiled the way a sleeping animal coils. Speak to it and it clears its throat first — a dry rasping shuffle of fiber against fiber, unmistakably the sound of somebody about to say something — and then it goes up the wall at the speed of a slow apology. It has never once made that sound at any other time.
items.hooks: Ropes like this are made in one valley and sold with a printed slip advising the buyer not to give the rope a name. This one has a name burned into a leather tag at the coil's heart, in a child's lettering, and it answers to it noticeably faster than it answers to being pointed at.
items.name: The Rope That Listens

dnd5e.mechanics: Once per day, speak to the rope and point: it climbs to a ledge, hook, beam, or branch within 50 feet and makes itself fast there. It is slow, it takes about a minute, and it anchors to the nearest thing it judges close enough — which is not always the thing you meant. 50 feet of hempen rope otherwise.

pf2e.mechanics: Once per day, command the rope and indicate a point within 50 feet; over about a minute it climbs and secures itself to the nearest suitable anchor, which may not be the one intended. Otherwise a 50-foot rope.

at_the_table: A weapon that quietly ruins whatever it's stored with is a logistics problem the player will actually roleplay: the cutlass travels lashed outside the pack.
Put it in a room where the water shouldn't run — a desert vault, an airless crypt — and let the players watch the fuller fill.
items.description: A heavy curved blade with a basket hilt gone green at the joins, and it beads water along the fuller no matter where it hangs — a slow sweat of it, cold, salt on the tongue, in a dry room a hundred miles inland. Wipe the blade and it beads again within the hour. The scabbard has been replaced four times and every one has rotted through from the inside.
items.hooks: Every dockside dealer on this coast knows the blade and none of them will keep it overnight. The salt it sweats has been tasted by people who would know, and they place it: not this sea, but the cold one four hundred miles north, where a ship called something else went down with a crew nobody has finished naming.
items.name: Tidebound Cutlass, +1 Scimitar

dnd5e.mechanics: +1 to attack and damage rolls. Base weapon: scimitar.

pf2e.mechanics: +1 striking scimitar.

at_the_table: The water problem is solved forever, which turns deserts, marshes, and sieges from survival math into terrain the party can cross at a walk.
The aftertaste is the DM's free hand: what the water was carrying is a fact the party learns by drinking, one mouthful before anyone has thought to ask.
items.description: A dented tin kettle with a wired-on handle, the kind that costs two silver anywhere in the world. Water comes out of it clean and cold and perfectly clear — and tasting, faintly and briefly, of whatever it stopped being. Marsh water comes out tasting of iron and old leaves; cistern water of dust; and once in a while a kettle of river water comes up tasting of nothing at all, which the crews on the fever rivers say is the one to be careful of.
items.hooks: Mission-posts issue these along the fever rivers and take them back when a post closes, which is how this one came to market. Its previous post kept a taste-log, as the posts do, in a ruled book of dates and single words: *leaves, iron, dust, iron, leaves.* The last four months of entries are all the same word, and the word is *salt*, and that river is three hundred miles from any sea.
items.name: Traveler's Kettle

dnd5e.mechanics: Water left in the kettle for 10 minutes becomes clean and safe to drink, whatever it was before — swamp, brine, cistern, blood. It holds a gallon and can be used any number of times. It doesn't counteract magical contamination or poison added deliberately.

pf2e.mechanics: Water left in the kettle for 10 minutes becomes potable regardless of its prior state. It holds a gallon and has no daily limit. It doesn't counteract magical contamination or deliberate poisoning.

at_the_table: The ration clock stops. A wilderness arc built on a countdown needs a new source of pressure, and the party has bought its way out of the oldest one in the genre.
A shaker like this makes the party quartermasters to whoever they meet next: a besieged garrison, a famine village, a becalmed ship. What they charge for it is a character sheet.
items.description: A stub of a shaker in tarnished pewter, gritty around the perforations, with a screw base nobody has ever managed to turn. What comes out is coarse gray salt that tastes of salt first and then, a beat later, of cold open water — a second note that stays in preserved food for as long as the food lasts, which is forever. Every cook who owns one learns to season around it.
items.hooks: A sealed larder came to light this spring under a collapsed manor house, and everything inside was edible — bread, a dressed fowl, a bowl of cut fruit, none of it a day old by taste. The manor came down forty years ago with the family still in it. The salt cellar on the shelf was empty, and the larder door had been barred from the inside.
items.name: Truesalt Shaker

dnd5e.mechanics: Food salted from the shaker never spoils, rots, or sours, and stays as fresh as the moment it was seasoned. It preserves only — food already spoiled stays spoiled. The shaker refills itself daily, yielding enough salt to keep about a week's provisions for four.

pf2e.mechanics: Food salted from the shaker never spoils and remains as fresh as when it was seasoned. It preserves only; already-spoiled food is unaffected. It refills daily, enough to keep roughly a week's provisions for four.

at_the_table: The cold-weather arc's small mercy, and a real question about who gets it: one stone, five sleepers, and nobody wants to be the one who asks.
Handed to a shivering prisoner, a sick child, or a scout who came in hostile, it does more diplomatic work than a speech.
items.description: A river-smoothed stone the size of a fist, gray-green and unremarkable, that warms in your hands within a breath and holds that warmth all night. Hold it near your face and it smells of woodsmoke and of bread coming out of an oven — a whole kitchen's worth of smell, off a bare stone, in a wet field, with nothing burning within ten miles. Most owners stop mentioning this part to strangers.
items.hooks: They turn up in trade far more often than anyone makes them, and always singly. A drover found this one last winter in a snowbank on the high pass, still warm, with no tracks within a hundred yards: a bare circle of green grass in six feet of snow, the stone sitting in the middle of it, smelling of somebody's kitchen.
items.name: Warmstone

dnd5e.mechanics: Tucked into a bedroll, the stone gives off steady body heat for 8 hours, then needs a day in daylight before it works again. One sleeper benefits: a cold night's rest counts as an ordinary one for them.

pf2e.mechanics: Tucked into a bedroll, the stone gives off steady body heat for 8 hours, then needs a day in daylight to function again. One sleeper benefits, resting through cold weather as though sheltered.

at_the_table: An hour is exactly enough to make camp, reef a sail, or decide to push on anyway. Weather stops being a DM announcement and becomes a party decision.
Sailors, drovers, and siege engineers all want one and none of them can afford three, so the wearer becomes the person everyone consults — and blames.
items.description: A copper vane no bigger than a coin, hung on a fine chain, and it will not hang straight. Level the chain, weight the end, lay the whole thing flat on a table — it settles a few degrees off, every time, and always the same few degrees. When weather is coming you feel it before you see it: a slow cold turn in the metal against your breastbone, about an hour ahead of the sky agreeing with it.
items.hooks: Harbor masters pay well for these and log every warning acted on, because an hour saves ships. One port's log carries a single entry with no weather written beside it: the charm turned cold, the master cleared the quay, and the sky stayed flat and blue all afternoon. The wave came in at dusk out of that calm and took the empty quay with it.
items.name: Weathervane Charm

dnd5e.mechanics: Worn openly, the charm gives its wearer about an hour's warning of any significant change in the weather — rain, snow, squall, or a storm breaking. It reports what is coming and roughly when, and nothing else.

pf2e.mechanics: Worn openly, the charm warns its wearer about an hour before any significant weather change — rain, snow, squall, or a breaking storm. It conveys what is coming and roughly when, and nothing further.
